**Fort Hill High School** is a four-year public high school in Cumberland, Maryland, United States, serving 780 students in grades 9 through 12. Fort Hill is part of Allegany County Public Schools**.**
Fort Hill High School was one of three local New Deal projects. Fort Hill High school was a Public Works Administration project. Nearby Constitution Park and Greeway Avenue Stadium were Works Progress Administration projects
New Deal funding relating to Fort Hill was initiated in November 1934 and September 1935, when the PWA committed federal funds not to exceed $230,000. The project was labeled PWA Docket #7323.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-2)

When Fort Hill opened, it had 1763 students and 88 teachers. Heisey was the first principal.

### State championships
[edit]
**Boys Cross Country:**
*   Class 2A 1995, 1997[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-auto1-3)
**Football:**
*   Class 3A 1975 (undefeated)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-auto1-3)  
*   Class 2A 1997 (undefeated)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-auto1-3)  
*   Class 1A 2013 (undefeated), 2014 (undefeated), 2015, 2016 (undefeated), 2018 (undefeated), 2021 (undefeated), 2022, 2023 (undefeated), 2024 [[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-auto1-3)
**Volleyball:**
*   Class 1A 2013[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-auto1-3)
The school has fielded a team since 1936, playing 925 total games (726 wins, 182 losses, 17 ties), producing an all-time winning percentage of 79% as of 2021.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-4)

### State championships
*   Fort Hill has won 11 state football championships since the inception of the Maryland Public Secondary Schools Athletic Association state playoffs in 1974. By decade:   
    *   1975 (3A)  
    *   1997 (2A)  
    *   2013 (1A), 2014 (1A), 2015 (1A), 2016 (1A), 2018 (1A)  
    *   2021 (1A), 2022 (1A), 2023 (1A), 2024 (1A).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-6)

*   Fort Hill has a Maryland state record of most undefeated regular seasons at 21:   
    *   **40s-60s:** 1948, 1950, 1957, 1958, 1963,  
    *   **70s-90s:** 1973, 1975, 1977, 1990, 1994, 1995, 1997  
    *   **2000-2020:** 2000, 2009, 2011, 2013, 2014, 2016, 2018  
    *   **Since 2021:** 2021, 2023.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-7)

### State championships
*   Fort Hill has a Maryland state record of most undefeated seasons overall at 14:   
    *   **40s-60s:** 1948, 1950, 1957, 1958, 1963  
    *   **70s-90s:** 1973, 1975, 1997  
    *   **2000s:** 2013, 2014, 2016, 2018, 2021, 2023.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-8)
The school gymnasium is used for league basketball.
Greenway Avenue Stadium, located at the school, was constructed in the 1930s by the Public Works Administration as part of President Roosevelt's New Deal and was built for the high school as _Fort Hill Stadium_. The stadium, since renamed as Greenway Avenue stadium and shared with Allegany High School, is considered to be an historic landmark. A $7 million renovation project to update and expand the 70-year-old facility has been completed.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-9)
*   Rebeca Arthur, actress[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-10)  
*   James Deetz, archeologist[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-11)  
*   Ty Johnson (American football), running back[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-12)  
*   Mark Manges, quarterback[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-13)  
*   Steve Trimble, NFL free safety (Denver Broncos 1981–1983, Chicago Bears 1987)

BUILT ON TRADITION. DEFINED BY GREATNESS.
FORT HILL SENTINELS | CUMBERLAND, MARYLAND
When you talk about the history of Maryland high school football, you can’t leave out the Fort Hill Sentinels!
One of the most decorated football programs in Maryland, Fort Hill has built a legacy of championship excellence, toughness, discipline, and a winning tradition that spans generations.
11 STATE CHAMPIONSHIPS
8 STATE RUNNER-UP FINISHES
12 STATE SEMIFINAL APPEARANCES
Cumberland, Maryland
Class 1A West
From their first state championship in 1975 to their most recent title in 2024, the Sentinels have continued to prove why they’re one of the state’s most respected football powerhouses.
Different generations. Same tradition. Same standard.
MHSS QUESTION: Where does Fort Hill rank among the greatest high school football programs in Maryland history?

**Fort Hill High School** is a four-year public high school in Cumberland, Maryland, United States, serving 780 students in grades 9 through 12. Fort Hill is part of Allegany County Public Schools**.**
Fort Hill High School was one of three local New Deal projects. Fort Hill High school was a Public Works Administration project. Nearby Constitution Park and Greeway Avenue Stadium were Works Progress Administration projects
New Deal funding relating to Fort Hill was initiated in November 1934 and September 1935, when the PWA committed federal funds not to exceed $230,000. The project was labeled PWA Docket #7323.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-2)
texts.1: When Fort Hill opened, it had 1763 students and 88 teachers. Heisey was the first principal.
texts.2:
### State championships
[edit]
**Boys Cross Country:**
*   Class 2A 1995, 1997[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-auto1-3)
**Football:**
*   Class 3A 1975 (undefeated)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-auto1-3)  
*   Class 2A 1997 (undefeated)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-auto1-3)  
*   Class 1A 2013 (undefeated), 2014 (undefeated), 2015, 2016 (undefeated), 2018 (undefeated), 2021 (undefeated), 2022, 2023 (undefeated), 2024 [[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-auto1-3)
**Volleyball:**
*   Class 1A 2013[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-auto1-3)
The school has fielded a team since 1936, playing 925 total games (726 wins, 182 losses, 17 ties), producing an all-time winning percentage of 79% as of 2021.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-4)
texts.3:
### State championships
*   Fort Hill has won 11 state football championships since the inception of the Maryland Public Secondary Schools Athletic Association state playoffs in 1974. By decade:   
    *   1975 (3A)  
    *   1997 (2A)  
    *   2013 (1A), 2014 (1A), 2015 (1A), 2016 (1A), 2018 (1A)  
    *   2021 (1A), 2022 (1A), 2023 (1A), 2024 (1A).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-6)

*   Fort Hill has a Maryland state record of most undefeated regular seasons at 21:   
    *   **40s-60s:** 1948, 1950, 1957, 1958, 1963,  
    *   **70s-90s:** 1973, 1975, 1977, 1990, 1994, 1995, 1997  
    *   **2000-2020:** 2000, 2009, 2011, 2013, 2014, 2016, 2018  
    *   **Since 2021:** 2021, 2023.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-7)
texts.4:
### State championships
*   Fort Hill has a Maryland state record of most undefeated seasons overall at 14:   
    *   **40s-60s:** 1948, 1950, 1957, 1958, 1963  
    *   **70s-90s:** 1973, 1975, 1997  
    *   **2000s:** 2013, 2014, 2016, 2018, 2021, 2023.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-8)
The school gymnasium is used for league basketball.
Greenway Avenue Stadium, located at the school, was constructed in the 1930s by the Public Works Administration as part of President Roosevelt's New Deal and was built for the high school as _Fort Hill Stadium_. The stadium, since renamed as Greenway Avenue stadium and shared with Allegany High School, is considered to be an historic landmark. A $7 million renovation project to update and expand the 70-year-old facility has been completed.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-9)
*   Rebeca Arthur, actress[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-10)  
*   James Deetz, archeologist[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-11)  
*   Ty Johnson (American football), running back[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-12)  
*   Mark Manges, quarterback[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-13)  
*   Steve Trimble, NFL free safety (Denver Broncos 1981–1983, Chicago Bears 1987)

FORT HILL SENTINELS | CUMBERLAND, MARYLAND
When you talk about the history of Maryland high school football, you can’t leave out the Fort Hill Sentinels!
One of the most decorated football programs in Maryland, Fort Hill has built a legacy of championship excellence, toughness, discipline, and a winning tradition that spans generations.

**Fort Hill High School** is a four-year public high school in Cumberland, Maryland, United States, serving 780 students in grades 9 through 12. Fort Hill is part of Allegany County Public Schools**.**
Fort Hill High School was one of three local New Deal projects. Fort Hill High school was a Public Works Administration project. Nearby Constitution Park and Greeway Avenue Stadium were Works Progress Administration projects
New Deal funding relating to Fort Hill was initiated in November 1934 and September 1935, when the PWA committed federal funds not to exceed $230,000. The project was labeled PWA Docket #7323.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-2)

When Fort Hill opened, it had 1763 students and 88 teachers. Heisey was the first principal.

### State championships
[edit]
**Boys Cross Country:**
*   Class 2A 1995, 1997[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-auto1-3)
**Football:**
*   Class 3A 1975 (undefeated)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-auto1-3)  
*   Class 2A 1997 (undefeated)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-auto1-3)  
*   Class 1A 2013 (undefeated), 2014 (undefeated), 2015, 2016 (undefeated), 2018 (undefeated), 2021 (undefeated), 2022, 2023 (undefeated), 2024 [[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-auto1-3)
**Volleyball:**
*   Class 1A 2013[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-auto1-3)
The school has fielded a team since 1936, playing 925 total games (726 wins, 182 losses, 17 ties), producing an all-time winning percentage of 79% as of 2021.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-4)

### State championships
*   Fort Hill has won 11 state football championships since the inception of the Maryland Public Secondary Schools Athletic Association state playoffs in 1974. By decade:   
    *   1975 (3A)  
    *   1997 (2A)  
    *   2013 (1A), 2014 (1A), 2015 (1A), 2016 (1A), 2018 (1A)  
    *   2021 (1A), 2022 (1A), 2023 (1A), 2024 (1A).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-6)

*   Fort Hill has a Maryland state record of most undefeated regular seasons at 21:   
    *   **40s-60s:** 1948, 1950, 1957, 1958, 1963,  
    *   **70s-90s:** 1973, 1975, 1977, 1990, 1994, 1995, 1997  
    *   **2000-2020:** 2000, 2009, 2011, 2013, 2014, 2016, 2018  
    *   **Since 2021:** 2021, 2023.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-7)

### State championships
*   Fort Hill has a Maryland state record of most undefeated seasons overall at 14:   
    *   **40s-60s:** 1948, 1950, 1957, 1958, 1963  
    *   **70s-90s:** 1973, 1975, 1997  
    *   **2000s:** 2013, 2014, 2016, 2018, 2021, 2023.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-8)
The school gymnasium is used for league basketball.
Greenway Avenue Stadium, located at the school, was constructed in the 1930s by the Public Works Administration as part of President Roosevelt's New Deal and was built for the high school as _Fort Hill Stadium_. The stadium, since renamed as Greenway Avenue stadium and shared with Allegany High School, is considered to be an historic landmark. A $7 million renovation project to update and expand the 70-year-old facility has been completed.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_High_School#cite_note-9)

[October 30 at 4:55 PM](https://www.facebook.com/senatorgeorgeborrello/posts/pfbid0KugfNJfsie5cpHcFHagHYCnCrf24hhtiXKvECNVJoWpXRPc6yGpY3wRF8ddCRUXtl?__cft__[0]=AZjRaxJfUH5LJI_6ptyPypGIYS5sHr_2kBtCoEkjIvArMUk4z0XAHxDHYkrqkgadGGJqs-VTRSDAa-SRbkXTpETgzu0PF0WfrraZ9SFxy-6U8m7WTOjSgSpw4A0_GUBGRBNicx2JPg9LQUCmXP9Wo8S_rJxOozX3&__tn__=%2CO%2CP-R) ·
Great news for Genesee County and American manufacturing!
The completion of Edwards Vacuum’s new $319 million advanced manufacturing facility at the STAMP site in the Town of Alabama is a major milestone for our region. The facility will produce critical equipment used in semiconductor chip manufacturing and is expected to create hundreds of good-paying jobs.
However, this investment is about more than jobs. It's about strengthening America's national and economic security by reducing our dependence on China and other foreign countries for advanced semiconductor manufacturing. As President Trump has emphasized, reshoring critical manufacturing and regaining control of our supply chains must be national priorities. This facility is an important part of that effort.
I want to thank Genesee County's economic development leaders, our federal and state partners and everyone whose hard work and collaboration helped make this project a reality.
This is exactly the kind of investment we need to strengthen our manufacturing economy, create opportunities for our residents and secure America's technological future.

## Advancing Sustainable Dry Pump Manufacturing
Edwards Genesee is a cutting-edge dry pump manufacturing facility designed to strengthen the U.S. semiconductor supply chain and drive innovation in advanced manufacturing. Located in Genesee County, New York, and set to begin operations in 2026, the facility will feature state-of-the-art vacuum pump technology and precision measurement systems. By producing high-performance dry pumps essential for semiconductor fabrication, Edwards Genesee will improve production efficiency, reduce downtime, and support cleanroom operations across the industry. This strategic investment will create approximately 280 skilled jobs, promote sustainable manufacturing practices, and contribute to the growth of the local economy. As a key player in semiconductor equipment manufacturing, Edwards Genesee is committed to powering the future of microelectronics and supporting the global demand for reliable, energy-efficient vacuum solutions.

## Facility Highlights
Edwards Vacuum, a global leader in vacuum and abatement solutions and part of Atlas Copco Group, has celebrated the official opening of its new Genesee manufacturing facility in Western New York.
The facility represents Atlas Copco Group’s continued investment in US manufacturing and semiconductor supply chain infrastructure, helping strengthen America's ability to produce critical technologies domestically while supporting the continued growth of the semiconductor industry.
Purpose-built to produce the advanced dry vacuum pumps used in semiconductor manufacturing, the Genesee facility expands Edwards' North American production capabilities and will cater for the demand driven by investments in semiconductor manufacturing across the US. Powered by renewable hydroelectric energy generated from nearby Niagara Falls, the facility combines advanced manufacturing capabilities with Edwards' commitment to sustainability, innovation, and long-term regional investment.
The Genesee site will support customers across North America and around the world while creating high-quality manufacturing, engineering, and technical career opportunities in Western New York. The investment further strengthens the region's growing position within the semiconductor and advanced manufacturing ecosystem.
The project is the result of strong collaboration between industry, government, economic development organizations, educational institutions, and community stakeholders. Edwards also recognizes the contributions of regional partners whose support helped advance the project and reinforce Western New York's growing role in the semiconductor industry.
The Genesee opening reflects Atlas Copco Group's continued investment in North American manufacturing and innovation. The Genesee facility is actively hiring to build their workforce; please use this link to review current open positions: Genesee - Search Jobs | Atlas Copco Group

## Facility Status
The Genesee County facility has successfully moved from construction into final readiness and operational setup.
Following the Temporary Certificate of Occupancy received in mid‑January and Substantial Completion shortly thereafter, teams moved into the building in early February. Since then, focus has shifted to finishing activities and preparing the facility for full use.
Inside, the space has continued to take shape. Office furniture and kitchen equipment are installed, branding elements including signage and wall graphics are in place, and all major production equipment is fully installed. Utility connections and system validations have progressed steadily across the facility.
With commissioning complete and teams actively working onsite, the facility is now positioned for its official opening later this year.

## Genesee Goes Airborne
A major milestone in the development of the Genesee facility was achieved with the successful helicopter-assisted installation of critical rooftop infrastructure. Utilizing aerial lift operations, heavy mechanical systems were precisely positioned enabling efficient deployment in areas inaccessible by ground-based cranes.
This approach not only improved installation efficiency and safety but also minimized disruption to the surrounding site and community.

## Meet the Genesee Staff
### Dan Papsidero
##### General Manager - Product Company Genesee
Dan serves as General Manager for Product Company Genesee, strengthening the Semiconductor division’s operational team through his leadership and drive.
He has proven experience in operational excellence, quality, design engineering, and continual improvement across industries including aerospace electro-mechanical and hydraulic flight control systems. His combination of operational experience and business acumen supports continued performance and growth.
He holds a Master of Business Administration from Boston College, a Master of Engineering from the Rochester Institute of Technology and is a certified Lean Six Sigma Black Belt practitioner.
Dan is married with two children. Outside of work, he works on his family farm where he has horses and chickens. His hobbies include golfing, exercising, and attending Buffalo Bills football games.

## Meet the Genesee Staff
### Jasmina B.
##### HR Manager - Product Company Genesee
Appointed HR Manager for Product Company Genesee in June 2025, Jasmina is responsible for leading HR operations, strategic workforce planning, and compliance. She reports directly to Dan Papsidero.
Since joining Edwards Vacuum in 2018 as an HR Generalist in the General Vacuum Division, Jasmina has held progressive roles including Mergers & Acquisitions, Integration HR Manager in the Semiconductor Division. She has been a key leader in the development of PC Genesee, driving the People & Culture and Learning & Development workstreams. She has ten years of Humam Resources experience in the manufacturing sector with strong expertise in project management, organizational design, compliance, and change management.
Jasmina holds a B.S. in Healthcare Administration from SUNY Brockport and is certified as a Professional in Human Resources (PHR).
Outside of work, Jasmina enjoys traveling and spending time with family.

## Meet the Genesee Staff
### Paul Marchetti
##### Business Controller - Product Company Genesee
In his role as Business Controller, Paul is responsible for supporting the financial oversight, strategic planning, and performance management of Genesee operations.
Paul brings a deep understanding of the business and a strong track record of success within the organization. Most recently, he served as VTBA Logistics Business Controller, managing the financial reporting strategy of distribution center networks across North America, China, Korea, and Japan. Prior to that, he held roles as Business Controller for Edwards North America General Vacuum and Business Controller for PC Niagara.
Paul holds a BA in International Business and Spanish and an MBA in Professional Accounting from Canisius College, as well as an MA in Hispanic Linguistics from the University at Buffalo.
Outside of work, Paul enjoys traveling and spending time with his two children, Dean and Alessandra.

## Meet the Genesee Staff
### Jerome Scharlau
##### Quality Manager - Product Company Genesee
Jerome serves as Quality Manager, overseeing the alignment of the quality management system with ISO standards and driving compliance and operational efficiency across the organization.
He has over 25 years of experience in engineering and quality systems, having held roles at Amada Tool America, ET Precision Optics, Woodward HSC, and Harris Corporation. His background spans process engineering, product development, and mechanical systems.
Jerome holds a Bachelor of Science in Mechanical Engineering from the Rochester Institute of Technology and an Associate of Science in Engineering Science from Genesee Community College.
Outside of work, he enjoys carpentry, boating, gardening, and exploring history.

## Meet the Genesee Staff
### James Annunziata
##### Operations Manager - Product Company Genesee
James (Jamie) Annunziata serves as Operations Manager at Edwards Genesee, focusing on enhancing manufacturing efficiency and streamlining operational processes. He plays a key role in driving productivity, reducing costs, and supporting strategic growth across global operations.
Jamie brings 19 years of experience from Moog, where he served as Value Stream Manager for the F35 program as well as Pumps and Motors. His background includes lean manufacturing, process improvement, and cross-functional leadership.
Jamie holds a bachelor’s degree in business management and an MBA from Medaille University.
Outside of work, Jamie is a passionate hockey player and recently won a gold medal representing Team USA at the World Championships held at Buffalo Riverworks in June 2025. He will compete again in the Dominican Republic this November and enjoys supporting Buffalo sports and spending time with his family.

## Meet the Genesee Staff
### Joshua Kubera
##### EHS Manager - Product Company Genesee
Joshua leads the Environmental, Health & Safety (EHS) program and oversees Facilities Maintenance, helping to foster a strong safety culture and drive operational excellence across Edwards Genesee.
He brings experience from both the food and automotive industries, including his most recent role at Alkegen in the automotive insulation business unit.
Joshua holds a Bachelor of Science in Business Management and Sport Management from SUNY Fredonia and a Master of Science in EHS Management from Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT).
Outside the workplace, Joshua enjoys staying active and spending time outdoors. He is a regular at the gym and a devoted sports fan, cheering on the Pittsburgh Pirates and the Dallas Cowboys.

# Great news for Genesee County... - Senator George Borrello | Facebook
[October 30 at 4:55 PM](https://www.facebook.com/senatorgeorgeborrello/posts/pfbid0KugfNJfsie5cpHcFHagHYCnCrf24hhtiXKvECNVJoWpXRPc6yGpY3wRF8ddCRUXtl?__cft__[0]=AZjRaxJfUH5LJI_6ptyPypGIYS5sHr_2kBtCoEkjIvArMUk4z0XAHxDHYkrqkgadGGJqs-VTRSDAa-SRbkXTpETgzu0PF0WfrraZ9SFxy-6U8m7WTOjSgSpw4A0_GUBGRBNicx2JPg9LQUCmXP9Wo8S_rJxOozX3&__tn__=%2CO%2CP-R) ·
Great news for Genesee County and American manufacturing!
The completion of Edwards Vacuum’s new $319 million advanced manufacturing facility at the STAMP site in the Town of Alabama is a major milestone for our region. The facility will produce critical equipment used in semiconductor chip manufacturing and is expected to create hundreds of good-paying jobs.
However, this investment is about more than jobs. It's about strengthening America's national and economic security by reducing our dependence on China and other foreign countries for advanced semiconductor manufacturing. As President Trump has emphasized, reshoring critical manufacturing and regaining control of our supply chains must be national priorities. This facility is an important part of that effort.
I want to thank Genesee County's economic development leaders, our federal and state partners and everyone whose hard work and collaboration helped make this project a reality.
This is exactly the kind of investment we need to strengthen our manufacturing economy, create opportunities for our residents and secure America's technological future.

# Edwards Haverhill Facility
## A Golden Achievement
Atlas Copco built the PC Haverhill facility with sustainability in mind.
It’s with that level of commitment and care for our planet that we are very proud to share some exciting news. Edwards Vacuum (PC Haverhill) has officially achieved its LEED Gold Certification following acceptance of the Design and Construction Final Review.
LEED Gold certification represents a significant achievement in sustainable building practices, and indicates that a building has met stringent sustainability criteria and demonstrates a commitment to environmental stewardship.

# Edwards Haverhill Facility
## Cryo Crew Softball is a Hit
Sharing quality time outside the office with fellow employees and being a part of the Haverhill community is what this team is all about. Improving the culture and bringing the facility together through wellbeing and inclusion.
The Cryo Crew is the only softball team in Haverill's Recreation League made up entirely of employees from the same company. In doing so, the team embraced their diversity and welcomed inclusion. They actually found strength in their differences, and celebrated the small victories of the team..
Even when the loses piled up, the teams attitude became stronger, and the team grew stronger. It wasnt about winning, it was about the comradely, the team building, the inclusion and diversity, and most of all, the fun of playing a simple game with your colleagues and enjoying their company.This simple mindset has made the Cryo Crew stronger and resilient. It has kick-started something that you can feel in the culture at Edwards PC Haverhill, and this is just the beginning.

## Advancing Sustainable Dry Pump Manufacturing
Edwards Genesee is a cutting-edge dry pump manufacturing facility designed to strengthen the U.S. semiconductor supply chain and drive innovation in advanced manufacturing. Located in Genesee County, New York, and set to begin operations in 2026, the facility will feature state-of-the-art vacuum pump technology and precision measurement systems. By producing high-performance dry pumps essential for semiconductor fabrication, Edwards Genesee will improve production efficiency, reduce downtime, and support cleanroom operations across the industry. This strategic investment will create approximately 280 skilled jobs, promote sustainable manufacturing practices, and contribute to the growth of the local economy. As a key player in semiconductor equipment manufacturing, Edwards Genesee is committed to powering the future of microelectronics and supporting the global demand for reliable, energy-efficient vacuum solutions.

## Facility Highlights
Edwards Vacuum, a global leader in vacuum and abatement solutions and part of Atlas Copco Group, has celebrated the official opening of its new Genesee manufacturing facility in Western New York.
The facility represents Atlas Copco Group’s continued investment in US manufacturing and semiconductor supply chain infrastructure, helping strengthen America's ability to produce critical technologies domestically while supporting the continued growth of the semiconductor industry.
Purpose-built to produce the advanced dry vacuum pumps used in semiconductor manufacturing, the Genesee facility expands Edwards' North American production capabilities and will cater for the demand driven by investments in semiconductor manufacturing across the US. Powered by renewable hydroelectric energy generated from nearby Niagara Falls, the facility combines advanced manufacturing capabilities with Edwards' commitment to sustainability, innovation, and long-term regional investment.
The Genesee site will support customers across North America and around the world while creating high-quality manufacturing, engineering, and technical career opportunities in Western New York. The investment further strengthens the region's growing position within the semiconductor and advanced manufacturing ecosystem.
The project is the result of strong collaboration between industry, government, economic development organizations, educational institutions, and community stakeholders. Edwards also recognizes the contributions of regional partners whose support helped advance the project and reinforce Western New York's growing role in the semiconductor industry.
The Genesee opening reflects Atlas Copco Group's continued investment in North American manufacturing and innovation. The Genesee facility is actively hiring to build their workforce; please use this link to review current open positions: Genesee - Search Jobs | Atlas Copco Group

## Facility Status
The Genesee County facility has successfully moved from construction into final readiness and operational setup.
Following the Temporary Certificate of Occupancy received in mid‑January and Substantial Completion shortly thereafter, teams moved into the building in early February. Since then, focus has shifted to finishing activities and preparing the facility for full use.
Inside, the space has continued to take shape. Office furniture and kitchen equipment are installed, branding elements including signage and wall graphics are in place, and all major production equipment is fully installed. Utility connections and system validations have progressed steadily across the facility.
With commissioning complete and teams actively working onsite, the facility is now positioned for its official opening later this year.

## Genesee Goes Airborne
A major milestone in the development of the Genesee facility was achieved with the successful helicopter-assisted installation of critical rooftop infrastructure. Utilizing aerial lift operations, heavy mechanical systems were precisely positioned enabling efficient deployment in areas inaccessible by ground-based cranes.
This approach not only improved installation efficiency and safety but also minimized disruption to the surrounding site and community.

## Meet the Genesee Staff
### Dan Papsidero
##### General Manager - Product Company Genesee
Dan serves as General Manager for Product Company Genesee, strengthening the Semiconductor division’s operational team through his leadership and drive.
He has proven experience in operational excellence, quality, design engineering, and continual improvement across industries including aerospace electro-mechanical and hydraulic flight control systems. His combination of operational experience and business acumen supports continued performance and growth.
He holds a Master of Business Administration from Boston College, a Master of Engineering from the Rochester Institute of Technology and is a certified Lean Six Sigma Black Belt practitioner.
Dan is married with two children. Outside of work, he works on his family farm where he has horses and chickens. His hobbies include golfing, exercising, and attending Buffalo Bills football games.

## Meet the Genesee Staff
### Jasmina B.
##### HR Manager - Product Company Genesee
Appointed HR Manager for Product Company Genesee in June 2025, Jasmina is responsible for leading HR operations, strategic workforce planning, and compliance. She reports directly to Dan Papsidero.
Since joining Edwards Vacuum in 2018 as an HR Generalist in the General Vacuum Division, Jasmina has held progressive roles including Mergers & Acquisitions, Integration HR Manager in the Semiconductor Division. She has been a key leader in the development of PC Genesee, driving the People & Culture and Learning & Development workstreams. She has ten years of Humam Resources experience in the manufacturing sector with strong expertise in project management, organizational design, compliance, and change management.
Jasmina holds a B.S. in Healthcare Administration from SUNY Brockport and is certified as a Professional in Human Resources (PHR).
Outside of work, Jasmina enjoys traveling and spending time with family.

## Meet the Genesee Staff
### Paul Marchetti
##### Business Controller - Product Company Genesee
In his role as Business Controller, Paul is responsible for supporting the financial oversight, strategic planning, and performance management of Genesee operations.
Paul brings a deep understanding of the business and a strong track record of success within the organization. Most recently, he served as VTBA Logistics Business Controller, managing the financial reporting strategy of distribution center networks across North America, China, Korea, and Japan. Prior to that, he held roles as Business Controller for Edwards North America General Vacuum and Business Controller for PC Niagara.
Paul holds a BA in International Business and Spanish and an MBA in Professional Accounting from Canisius College, as well as an MA in Hispanic Linguistics from the University at Buffalo.
Outside of work, Paul enjoys traveling and spending time with his two children, Dean and Alessandra.

## Meet the Genesee Staff
### Jerome Scharlau
##### Quality Manager - Product Company Genesee
Jerome serves as Quality Manager, overseeing the alignment of the quality management system with ISO standards and driving compliance and operational efficiency across the organization.
He has over 25 years of experience in engineering and quality systems, having held roles at Amada Tool America, ET Precision Optics, Woodward HSC, and Harris Corporation. His background spans process engineering, product development, and mechanical systems.
Jerome holds a Bachelor of Science in Mechanical Engineering from the Rochester Institute of Technology and an Associate of Science in Engineering Science from Genesee Community College.
Outside of work, he enjoys carpentry, boating, gardening, and exploring history.

## Meet the Genesee Staff
### James Annunziata
##### Operations Manager - Product Company Genesee
James (Jamie) Annunziata serves as Operations Manager at Edwards Genesee, focusing on enhancing manufacturing efficiency and streamlining operational processes. He plays a key role in driving productivity, reducing costs, and supporting strategic growth across global operations.
Jamie brings 19 years of experience from Moog, where he served as Value Stream Manager for the F35 program as well as Pumps and Motors. His background includes lean manufacturing, process improvement, and cross-functional leadership.
Jamie holds a bachelor’s degree in business management and an MBA from Medaille University.
Outside of work, Jamie is a passionate hockey player and recently won a gold medal representing Team USA at the World Championships held at Buffalo Riverworks in June 2025. He will compete again in the Dominican Republic this November and enjoys supporting Buffalo sports and spending time with his family.

## Meet the Genesee Staff
### Joshua Kubera
##### EHS Manager - Product Company Genesee
Joshua leads the Environmental, Health & Safety (EHS) program and oversees Facilities Maintenance, helping to foster a strong safety culture and drive operational excellence across Edwards Genesee.
He brings experience from both the food and automotive industries, including his most recent role at Alkegen in the automotive insulation business unit.
Joshua holds a Bachelor of Science in Business Management and Sport Management from SUNY Fredonia and a Master of Science in EHS Management from Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT).
Outside the workplace, Joshua enjoys staying active and spending time outdoors. He is a regular at the gym and a devoted sports fan, cheering on the Pittsburgh Pirates and the Dallas Cowboys.

# Edwards Haverhill Facility
## A Golden Achievement
Atlas Copco built the PC Haverhill facility with sustainability in mind.
It’s with that level of commitment and care for our planet that we are very proud to share some exciting news. Edwards Vacuum (PC Haverhill) has officially achieved its LEED Gold Certification following acceptance of the Design and Construction Final Review.
LEED Gold certification represents a significant achievement in sustainable building practices, and indicates that a building has met stringent sustainability criteria and demonstrates a commitment to environmental stewardship.

# Edwards Haverhill Facility
## A Golden Achievement
###### WELLBEING & INCLUSION


# Edwards Haverhill Facility
## Cryo Crew Softball is a Hit
Sharing quality time outside the office with fellow employees and being a part of the Haverhill community is what this team is all about. Improving the culture and bringing the facility together through wellbeing and inclusion.
The Cryo Crew is the only softball team in Haverill's Recreation League made up entirely of employees from the same company. In doing so, the team embraced their diversity and welcomed inclusion. They actually found strength in their differences, and celebrated the small victories of the team..
Even when the loses piled up, the teams attitude became stronger, and the team grew stronger. It wasnt about winning, it was about the comradely, the team building, the inclusion and diversity, and most of all, the fun of playing a simple game with your colleagues and enjoying their company.This simple mindset has made the Cryo Crew stronger and resilient. It has kick-started something that you can feel in the culture at Edwards PC Haverhill, and this is just the beginning.

**Shelia Edwards** is an American politician, and businesswoman who is currently a member-elect of the Georgia Public Service Commission (PSC). A member of the Democratic Party of Georgia, Edwards first ran for the position in 2022, but was forced to end her campaign when the elections were cancelled by a court. She ran again in 2026 and defeated her Republican opponent.

### Georgia Public Service Commission
[edit]
Edwards first ran for a seat on the PSC in 2022, and won the Democratic primary.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelia_Edwards#cite_note-1) The 2022 elections were postponed due to a court ruling, and were not held again until 2025.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelia_Edwards#cite_note-2)
Edwards chose to run in 2026, to represent the 5th district. PSC elections in Georgia are held statewide, regardless of district. Edwards won the Democratic primary outright on May 19.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelia_Edwards#cite_note-3) She defeated Josh Tolbert, the Republican nominee, on November 3rd with 55% of the vote. With her victory, Democrats flipped control of the commission for the first time in 30 years.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelia_Edwards#cite_note-4)
1.   ↑Nolin, Jill (July 13, 2022). "Democrats ask court to settle intraparty fight to face GOP's PSC nominee in fall". _Georgia Recorder_. Retrieved November 5, 2026.  
2.   ↑Williams, Dave (March 7, 2024). "Lawsuit again postpones elections to the Georgia commission that regulates power bill rates". _The Augusta Chronicle_. Retrieved November 5, 2026.  
3.   ↑Jones, Emily (May 20, 2026). "Democrat Shelia Edwards wins utility commission primary as Republicans head to a runoff". _WABE_. Retrieved November 5, 2026.  
4.   ↑Rocha, Alander (November 4, 2026). "Democrats gain control of Georgia board that regulates utilities for first time in decades". _Georgia Recorder_. Retrieved November 5, 2026.

Democratic presidential candidate John Edwards won the South Carolina primary in 2004, a victory he was unable to repeat in Saturday's contest. Despite the defeat, Edwards vows to continue his campaign, points to recent successes in fundraising and reiterates that the presidential nomination is a "long process." Edwards speaks to Liane Hansen about what lies ahead.

**Shelia Edwards** is an American politician, and businesswoman who is currently a member-elect of the Georgia Public Service Commission (PSC). A member of the Democratic Party of Georgia, Edwards first ran for the position in 2022, but was forced to end her campaign when the elections were cancelled by a court. She ran again in 2026 and defeated her Republican opponent.
texts.1:
### Georgia Public Service Commission
[edit]
Edwards first ran for a seat on the PSC in 2022, and won the Democratic primary.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelia_Edwards#cite_note-1) The 2022 elections were postponed due to a court ruling, and were not held again until 2025.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelia_Edwards#cite_note-2)
Edwards chose to run in 2026, to represent the 5th district. PSC elections in Georgia are held statewide, regardless of district. Edwards won the Democratic primary outright on May 19.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelia_Edwards#cite_note-3) She defeated Josh Tolbert, the Republican nominee, on November 3rd with 55% of the vote. With her victory, Democrats flipped control of the commission for the first time in 30 years.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelia_Edwards#cite_note-4)
1.   ↑Nolin, Jill (July 13, 2022). "Democrats ask court to settle intraparty fight to face GOP's PSC nominee in fall". _Georgia Recorder_. Retrieved November 5, 2026.  
2.   ↑Williams, Dave (March 7, 2024). "Lawsuit again postpones elections to the Georgia commission that regulates power bill rates". _The Augusta Chronicle_. Retrieved November 5, 2026.  
3.   ↑Jones, Emily (May 20, 2026). "Democrat Shelia Edwards wins utility commission primary as Republicans head to a runoff". _WABE_. Retrieved November 5, 2026.  
4.   ↑Rocha, Alander (November 4, 2026). "Democrats gain control of Georgia board that regulates utilities for first time in decades". _Georgia Recorder_. Retrieved November 5, 2026.

**Shelia Edwards** is an American politician, and businesswoman who is currently a member-elect of the Georgia Public Service Commission (PSC). A member of the Democratic Party of Georgia, Edwards first ran for the position in 2022, but was forced to end her campaign when the elections were cancelled by a court. She ran again in 2026 and defeated her Republican opponent.

### Georgia Public Service Commission
[edit]
Edwards first ran for a seat on the PSC in 2022, and won the Democratic primary.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelia_Edwards#cite_note-1) The 2022 elections were postponed due to a court ruling, and were not held again until 2025.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelia_Edwards#cite_note-2)
Edwards chose to run in 2026, to represent the 5th district. PSC elections in Georgia are held statewide, regardless of district. Edwards won the Democratic primary outright on May 19.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelia_Edwards#cite_note-3) She defeated Josh Tolbert, the Republican nominee, on November 3rd with 55% of the vote. With her victory, Democrats flipped control of the commission for the first time in 30 years.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelia_Edwards#cite_note-4)

# America’s Premier Skilled Trades Showcase
## Overview
The SkillsUSA Championships is the premier showcase of America’s most highly skilled career and technical education students. It’s also one of the largest hands-on workforce development events in the world. Held in conjunction with SkillsUSA’s National Leadership & Skills Conference each June, this awe-inspiring event features more than 7,000 state champions from across the United States competing head-to-head in 113 skilled and leadership competitions.
The event is held at the Georgia World Congress Center in Atlanta, and it covers over 1.79 million square feet of floor space, the equivalent of 31 football fields! The philosophy of the SkillsUSA Championships is to reward students for excellence, to involve industry in directly evaluating student performance and to keep classroom training relevant to employers’ needs.
Competitions are created, overseen, and judged by nearly 2,000 industry volunteers, each committed to building the next generation of skilled professionals, career-ready leaders and responsible community members on which our future depends. For more information, visit: Championships Official Operating Policies.
The SkillsUSA Championships is the national culmination of a year-long process that begins in local SkillsUSA chapters across the country. Local winners advance to district or regional competitions, testing their skills against competitors from other schools. Those winners advance to state competitions each spring, and state gold medalists earn the right to compete nationally at the SkillsUSA Championships each June. Along with gold, silver and bronze medallions, competitors may earn scholarships, tools of the trade, and even job offers right off the competition floor. Perhaps most importantly, they earn the confidence that can only come when you know you’re among the best of the best in what you do. For more information, visit: SkillsUSA Championships General Regulations.
If you’re wondering about the future of the skilled trades, look no further than the SkillsUSA Championships to see that it’s in good, highly skilled hands.

# America’s Premier Skilled Trades Showcase
## Volunteer at the National Competitions
Volunteer to Judge
We are looking for volunteers to assist with judging competitions on Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday during the week of the conference. Your support helps ensure a fair and successful SkillsUSA Championships!
For detailed information about the SkillsUSA Championships, see above. To view brief descriptions of each contest, click here.
If you are interested in serving as a volunteer, please fill out theinterest form. The form will open after April 1. Your contact information will be shared with technical chairs who have available volunteer positions. Thank you for your support!
Volunteer with National Courtesy Corps
SkillsUSA is seeking nominees for the National Courtesy Corps (NCC) program for the National Leadership & Skills Conference (NLSC). This program is a great opportunity for students and advisors to network with industry partners and experience the national conference in a unique way. NCC members receive free conference registration, housing, local transportation, and meals. To participate in this program, NCC candidates must work with their chapter advisor on meeting local travel requirements and seek approval of theirSkillsUSA State Director. Visit theNLSC micrositefor more information.
Volunteer as National Education Team Member
The National Education Team members play a critical role in supporting the National Technical Committees (NTCs) in the planning, administration, and management of SkillsUSA Championships competitions. NET members help communicate industry-aligned expectations for instructional quality and educator professional development within the occupational areas represented by their assigned competition.
Nominees should be current or retired educators with demonstrated expertise in the occupational area(s) for which they are nominated, as well as a proven record of active engagement and support of their state SkillsUSA conference.
Nominee qualifications will be reviewed by the state association director, the appropriate National Technical Committee, and the SkillsUSA Office of Workforce Development.
Additional information regarding responsibilities, selection criteria, and timelines is available on the NLSC microsite.

# America’s Premier Skilled Trades Showcase
## Overview
The SkillsUSA Championships is the premier showcase of America’s most highly skilled career and technical education students. It’s also one of the largest hands-on workforce development events in the world. Held in conjunction with SkillsUSA’s National Leadership & Skills Conference each June, this awe-inspiring event features more than 7,000 state champions from across the United States competing head-to-head in 113 skilled and leadership competitions.
The event is held at the Georgia World Congress Center in Atlanta, and it covers over 1.79 million square feet of floor space, the equivalent of 31 football fields! The philosophy of the SkillsUSA Championships is to reward students for excellence, to involve industry in directly evaluating student performance and to keep classroom training relevant to employers’ needs.
Competitions are created, overseen, and judged by nearly 2,000 industry volunteers, each committed to building the next generation of skilled professionals, career-ready leaders and responsible community members on which our future depends. For more information, visit: Championships Official Operating Policies.
The SkillsUSA Championships is the national culmination of a year-long process that begins in local SkillsUSA chapters across the country. Local winners advance to district or regional competitions, testing their skills against competitors from other schools. Those winners advance to state competitions each spring, and state gold medalists earn the right to compete nationally at the SkillsUSA Championships each June. Along with gold, silver and bronze medallions, competitors may earn scholarships, tools of the trade, and even job offers right off the competition floor. Perhaps most importantly, they earn the confidence that can only come when you know you’re among the best of the best in what you do. For more information, visit: SkillsUSA Championships General Regulations.
If you’re wondering about the future of the skilled trades, look no further than the SkillsUSA Championships to see that it’s in good, highly skilled hands.

# America’s Premier Skilled Trades Showcase
## Volunteer at the National Competitions
Volunteer to Judge
We are looking for volunteers to assist with judging competitions on Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday during the week of the conference. Your support helps ensure a fair and successful SkillsUSA Championships!
For detailed information about the SkillsUSA Championships, see above. To view brief descriptions of each contest, click here.
If you are interested in serving as a volunteer, please fill out theinterest form. The form will open after April 1. Your contact information will be shared with technical chairs who have available volunteer positions. Thank you for your support!
Volunteer with National Courtesy Corps
SkillsUSA is seeking nominees for the National Courtesy Corps (NCC) program for the National Leadership & Skills Conference (NLSC). This program is a great opportunity for students and advisors to network with industry partners and experience the national conference in a unique way. NCC members receive free conference registration, housing, local transportation, and meals. To participate in this program, NCC candidates must work with their chapter advisor on meeting local travel requirements and seek approval of theirSkillsUSA State Director. Visit theNLSC micrositefor more information.
Volunteer as National Education Team Member
The National Education Team members play a critical role in supporting the National Technical Committees (NTCs) in the planning, administration, and management of SkillsUSA Championships competitions. NET members help communicate industry-aligned expectations for instructional quality and educator professional development within the occupational areas represented by their assigned competition.
Nominees should be current or retired educators with demonstrated expertise in the occupational area(s) for which they are nominated, as well as a proven record of active engagement and support of their state SkillsUSA conference.
Nominee qualifications will be reviewed by the state association director, the appropriate National Technical Committee, and the SkillsUSA Office of Workforce Development.
Additional information regarding responsibilities, selection criteria, and timelines is available on the NLSC microsite.

Title: Fort Hill: National Historic Landmark
Chunks: 0,1
Prior to the Revolutionary War, the Cherokee called the land Esseneca. William Bartram visited this Lower Town twice, writing that it “is a respectable settlement, situated on the East Bank of the Keowee river.”
Before Fort Hill, the antebellum plantation of John C. Calhoun, South Carolina’s pre-eminent 19th century statesman, there was four-room Clergy Hall. Originally built in 1803, Clergy Hall served as the manse or parsonage for nearby Hopewell-Keowee Church, now known as Old Stone Presbyterian Church. Next, Floride Bonneau Colhoun, John C. Calhoun’s mother-in-law, purchased the 600 acre property; U.S. Vice President Calhoun’s family called the expanded structure Fort Hill, starting in 1830, after Revolutionary War Fort Rutledge.
In total, ten rooms were added to the structure and additional acreage was purchased by John C. Calhoun; however, he was not the owner until 1836, after the death of his mother-in-law.When John C. died in 1850, his wife Floride became the sole owner of the Fort Hill home and 1,341 acres of land. When she passed in 1866, portions of the property then went to their daughter and sole surviving child, Anna Maria Calhoun, who had married Thomas Green Clemson in 1838. The Clemsons’ daughter, Floride Elizabeth, also inherited a portion. Tragically, Anna Calhoun Clemson did not take ownership of land until her two surviving children had already passed.
Anna Maria Calhoun Clemson willed her three-fourths share of Fort Hill to her husband, Thomas Clemson, with the caveat that he must die with a will. At Anna’s death in 1875, Thomas worked with two attorneys, James Rion and Richard Wright Simpson, to create his bequest that became Clemson University. If he had not, the granddaughter Floride Isabella Lee would have inherited the entire property in accordance with Anna Clemson’s will.

Through a succession of Calhoun-Clemson women, Fort Hill would come into Thomas Green Clemson’s possession. In 1888, Clemson bequeathed three-fourths of the Fort Hill plantation and $80,000 to the state of South Carolina for the establishment of a public scientific and agricultural college. He willed that Fort Hill “shall always be open for the inspection of visitors.”
Today, Fort Hill is just as Thomas Clemson envisioned — preserved, restored and open to the public for tours.
The enslaved African-Americans, whose story of resistance and resilience left little written records, built and operated from 1825 through 1865., Prior to Anna Clemson inheriting Fort Hill on January 21, 1872, Thomas Green Clemson began signing employment contracts in 1868 with former enslaved persons from Fort Hill and neighboring plantations.
**Freedman's Contracts**
Signed by Thomas Green Clemson
Life at Fort Hill, and all of its financial growth, was only possible because of the physical labor and sheer determination of the enslaved African Americans who toiled on the 450 acre cultivated land, producing maintaining the household, and performing construction of the plantation.
Since the enslaved who occupied Fort Hill left no written record, their perspective has been made virtually voiceless in history. In many cases, names and family connections are not known.
**African Americans at Fort Hill – Primary Documents**
1854 and 1865
Little is known about the families who were enslaved at Fort Hill by its three plantation era owners, John C. Calhoun, Floride Colhoun Calhoun, and Andrew Pickens Calhoun. There are records of a few family units, including: Sawney, his wife Tiller, and at least two of their children, Sawney Jr. and Issey; Daphne, her husband Bill Lawrence, and their children Susan Clemson Richardson and Benjamin; Sharper, his wife Caroline, and his daughter Tiller; and Nelly and her son Andy.
Read more about African Americans at Fort Hill.

**Fort Hill**, also known as the **John C. Calhoun House and Library**, is a National Historic Landmark on the Clemson University campus in Pickens County, South Carolina, United States, near the City of Clemson.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_(Clemson_University,_South_Carolina)#cite_note-Censusmaps-4)
From 1825-1850, the house was the home of noted proponent of slavery and constitutional Nullification, John C. Calhoun, the 7th Vice President of the United States.

Clemson University was established on the Fort Hill slave-operated plantation site in 1889, and in accordance with the terms of its inheritance, has maintained the house and its immediate parcel as a museum and library — all that remains of what originally was an approximately 1,000 acre plantation estate.
Fort Hill
State historic marker for Fort Hill
The house was originally built as a four-room house about 1803 and was called **Clergy Hall** by Dr. James McElhenny, who was the pastor of Hopewell Presbyterian Church. The house later became the home of John C. Calhoun and his wife Floride Calhoun in 1825. Calhoun enlarged it to 14 rooms and renamed it Fort Hill for nearby Fort Rutledge, which was built around 1776. The architectural style is Greek Revival with Federal detailing and with simple interior detailing.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_(Clemson_University,_South_Carolina)#cite_note-5)
After John Calhoun's death in 1850, the property and the 50 slaves there passed to his wife to be shared with three of her children: Cornelia, John, and Anna Maria, wife of Thomas Green Clemson. Anna sold her share to Floride Calhoun. Floride Calhoun sold the plantation to her son, Andrew Pickens Calhoun, and held the mortgage. After Andrew died in 1865, she filed for foreclosure against Andrew's heirs before her death in 1866.
After lengthy legal proceedings, the plantation was auctioned at Walhalla in 1872. The executor of her estate won the auction, which was divided among her surviving heirs. Her daughter, Anna Clemson, received the residence with about 814 acres (329 ha) and her great-granddaughter, Floride Isabella Lee, received about 288 acres (117 ha). Thomas Green and Anna Clemson moved into Fort Hill in 1872. After Anna's death in 1875, Thomas Green Clemson inherited Fort Hill.

In his 1888 will, Clemson bequeathed more than 814 acres (329 ha) of the Fort Hill estate to the State of South Carolina for an agricultural college with a stipulation that the dwelling house "shall never be torn down or altered; but shall be kept in repair with all articles of furniture and vesture...and shall always be open for inspection of visitors."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_(Clemson_University,_South_Carolina)#cite_note-6)Clemson University has operated Fort Hill as a house museum as stipulated in the will. The house is all that remains of what was once an extensive plantation estate.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_(Clemson_University,_South_Carolina)#cite_note-scdahsum-7)
The home was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1960.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_(Clemson_University,_South_Carolina)#cite_note-nrhpinv2-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_(Clemson_University,_South_Carolina)#cite_note-nhlsum-3)
Fort Hill was closed for a two-year restoration project and was reopened in the spring of 2003. Fort Hill was named a national treasure by the [Save America's Treasures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Save_America's_Treasures "Save America's Treasures") program,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_(Clemson_University,_South_Carolina)#cite_note-8) and its artifacts are currently_[when?_] undergoing a comprehensive conservation program funded by this federal grant and matching funds.

The Fort Hill complex is comprised of the dwelling house, Calhoun’s office, a reconstructed kitchen, and a springhouse.
(Clemson). The plantation home of John C. Calhoun, Fort Hill was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1960, an honor that was reconfirmed in 1975. Calhoun composed some of his most significant political works at Fort Hill, including his 1828 _South Carolina Exposition and Protest_ on constitutional compact theory and the 1831 _Fort Hill Address,_ which set forth his theory of nullification.
Calhoun acquired the 1,100-acre plantation in 1825. The core of the main house was erected about 1803 by Dr. James McElhenny, a local Presbyterian pastor, and was called Clergy Hall. Calhoun enlarged it to fourteen rooms and renamed it Fort Hill, named for a fortification built there around 1776. After Calhoun’s death in 1850 and the Civil War, the property passed to his son-in-law, Thomas Green Clemson. In his 1888 will, Clemson bequeathed more than 814 acres of the Fort Hill estate to the state of South Carolina for an agricultural college, with a stipulation that the dwelling house “shall never be torn down or altered; but shall be kept in repair with all the articles of furniture and vesture . . . and shall always be open for the inspection of visitors.” Since the creation of Clemson University in the 1890s, the school has operated Fort Hill as a house museum as stipulated in Clemson’s will.
The Fort Hill complex is comprised of the dwelling house, Calhoun’s office, a reconstructed kitchen, and a springhouse. Its architectural style is Greek revival with Federal detailing and with simple, yet elegant interior detailing. Furnishings include a rare Dolphin-style Federal horsehair sofa, a Duncan Phyfe dining table and chairs, and a mahogany sideboard given by Henry Clay and made of wood from the USS _Constitution._

The Fort Hill complex is comprised of the dwelling house, Calhoun’s office, a reconstructed kitchen, and a springhouse.
(Clemson). The plantation home of John C. Calhoun, Fort Hill was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1960, an honor that was reconfirmed in 1975. Calhoun composed some of his most significant political works at Fort Hill, including his 1828 _South Carolina Exposition and Protest_ on constitutional compact theory and the 1831 _Fort Hill Address,_ which set forth his theory of nullification.
Calhoun acquired the 1,100-acre plantation in 1825. The core of the main house was erected about 1803 by Dr. James McElhenny, a local Presbyterian pastor, and was called Clergy Hall. Calhoun enlarged it to fourteen rooms and renamed it Fort Hill, named for a fortification built there around 1776. After Calhoun’s death in 1850 and the Civil War, the property passed to his son-in-law, Thomas Green Clemson. In his 1888 will, Clemson bequeathed more than 814 acres of the Fort Hill estate to the state of South Carolina for an agricultural college, with a stipulation that the dwelling house “shall never be torn down or altered; but shall be kept in repair with all the articles of furniture and vesture . . . and shall always be open for the inspection of visitors.” Since the creation of Clemson University in the 1890s, the school has operated Fort Hill as a house museum as stipulated in Clemson’s will.
The Fort Hill complex is comprised of the dwelling house, Calhoun’s office, a reconstructed kitchen, and a springhouse. Its architectural style is Greek revival with Federal detailing and with simple, yet elegant interior detailing. Furnishings include a rare Dolphin-style Federal horsehair sofa, a Duncan Phyfe dining table and chairs, and a mahogany sideboard given by Henry Clay and made of wood from the USS _Constitution._

Prior to the Revolutionary War, the Cherokee called the land Esseneca. William Bartram visited this Lower Town twice, writing that it “is a respectable settlement, situated on the East Bank of the Keowee river.”
Before Fort Hill, the antebellum plantation of John C. Calhoun, South Carolina’s pre-eminent 19th century statesman, there was four-room Clergy Hall. Originally built in 1803, Clergy Hall served as the manse or parsonage for nearby Hopewell-Keowee Church, now known as Old Stone Presbyterian Church. Next, Floride Bonneau Colhoun, John C. Calhoun’s mother-in-law, purchased the 600 acre property; U.S. Vice President Calhoun’s family called the expanded structure Fort Hill, starting in 1830, after Revolutionary War Fort Rutledge.
In total, ten rooms were added to the structure and additional acreage was purchased by John C. Calhoun; however, he was not the owner until 1836, after the death of his mother-in-law.When John C. died in 1850, his wife Floride became the sole owner of the Fort Hill home and 1,341 acres of land. When she passed in 1866, portions of the property then went to their daughter and sole surviving child, Anna Maria Calhoun, who had married Thomas Green Clemson in 1838. The Clemsons’ daughter, Floride Elizabeth, also inherited a portion. Tragically, Anna Calhoun Clemson did not take ownership of land until her two surviving children had already passed.
Anna Maria Calhoun Clemson willed her three-fourths share of Fort Hill to her husband, Thomas Clemson, with the caveat that he must die with a will. At Anna’s death in 1875, Thomas worked with two attorneys, James Rion and Richard Wright Simpson, to create his bequest that became Clemson University. If he had not, the granddaughter Floride Isabella Lee would have inherited the entire property in accordance with Anna Clemson’s will.
texts.1:
Through a succession of Calhoun-Clemson women, Fort Hill would come into Thomas Green Clemson’s possession. In 1888, Clemson bequeathed three-fourths of the Fort Hill plantation and $80,000 to the state of South Carolina for the establishment of a public scientific and agricultural college. He willed that Fort Hill “shall always be open for the inspection of visitors.”
Today, Fort Hill is just as Thomas Clemson envisioned — preserved, restored and open to the public for tours.
The enslaved African-Americans, whose story of resistance and resilience left little written records, built and operated from 1825 through 1865., Prior to Anna Clemson inheriting Fort Hill on January 21, 1872, Thomas Green Clemson began signing employment contracts in 1868 with former enslaved persons from Fort Hill and neighboring plantations.
**Freedman's Contracts**
Signed by Thomas Green Clemson
Life at Fort Hill, and all of its financial growth, was only possible because of the physical labor and sheer determination of the enslaved African Americans who toiled on the 450 acre cultivated land, producing maintaining the household, and performing construction of the plantation.
Since the enslaved who occupied Fort Hill left no written record, their perspective has been made virtually voiceless in history. In many cases, names and family connections are not known.
**African Americans at Fort Hill – Primary Documents**
1854 and 1865
Little is known about the families who were enslaved at Fort Hill by its three plantation era owners, John C. Calhoun, Floride Colhoun Calhoun, and Andrew Pickens Calhoun. There are records of a few family units, including: Sawney, his wife Tiller, and at least two of their children, Sawney Jr. and Issey; Daphne, her husband Bill Lawrence, and their children Susan Clemson Richardson and Benjamin; Sharper, his wife Caroline, and his daughter Tiller; and Nelly and her son Andy.

**Fort Hill**, also known as the **John C. Calhoun House and Library**, is a National Historic Landmark on the Clemson University campus in Pickens County, South Carolina, United States, near the City of Clemson.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_(Clemson_University,_South_Carolina)#cite_note-Censusmaps-4)
From 1825-1850, the house was the home of noted proponent of slavery and constitutional Nullification, John C. Calhoun, the 7th Vice President of the United States.
texts.1:
Clemson University was established on the Fort Hill slave-operated plantation site in 1889, and in accordance with the terms of its inheritance, has maintained the house and its immediate parcel as a museum and library — all that remains of what originally was an approximately 1,000 acre plantation estate.
Fort Hill
State historic marker for Fort Hill
The house was originally built as a four-room house about 1803 and was called **Clergy Hall** by Dr. James McElhenny, who was the pastor of Hopewell Presbyterian Church. The house later became the home of John C. Calhoun and his wife Floride Calhoun in 1825. Calhoun enlarged it to 14 rooms and renamed it Fort Hill for nearby Fort Rutledge, which was built around 1776. The architectural style is Greek Revival with Federal detailing and with simple interior detailing.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_(Clemson_University,_South_Carolina)#cite_note-5)
After John Calhoun's death in 1850, the property and the 50 slaves there passed to his wife to be shared with three of her children: Cornelia, John, and Anna Maria, wife of Thomas Green Clemson. Anna sold her share to Floride Calhoun. Floride Calhoun sold the plantation to her son, Andrew Pickens Calhoun, and held the mortgage. After Andrew died in 1865, she filed for foreclosure against Andrew's heirs before her death in 1866.
After lengthy legal proceedings, the plantation was auctioned at Walhalla in 1872. The executor of her estate won the auction, which was divided among her surviving heirs. Her daughter, Anna Clemson, received the residence with about 814 acres (329 ha) and her great-granddaughter, Floride Isabella Lee, received about 288 acres (117 ha). Thomas Green and Anna Clemson moved into Fort Hill in 1872. After Anna's death in 1875, Thomas Green Clemson inherited Fort Hill.
texts.2:
In his 1888 will, Clemson bequeathed more than 814 acres (329 ha) of the Fort Hill estate to the State of South Carolina for an agricultural college with a stipulation that the dwelling house "shall never be torn down or altered; but shall be kept in repair with all articles of furniture and vesture...and shall always be open for inspection of visitors."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_(Clemson_University,_South_Carolina)#cite_note-6)Clemson University has operated Fort Hill as a house museum as stipulated in the will. The house is all that remains of what was once an extensive plantation estate.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_(Clemson_University,_South_Carolina)#cite_note-scdahsum-7)
The home was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1960.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_(Clemson_University,_South_Carolina)#cite_note-nrhpinv2-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_(Clemson_University,_South_Carolina)#cite_note-nhlsum-3)
Fort Hill was closed for a two-year restoration project and was reopened in the spring of 2003. Fort Hill was named a national treasure by the [Save America's Treasures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Save_America's_Treasures "Save America's Treasures") program,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_(Clemson_University,_South_Carolina)#cite_note-8) and its artifacts are currently_[when?_] undergoing a comprehensive conservation program funded by this federal grant and matching funds.

When she passed in 1866, portions of the property then went to their daughter and sole surviving child, Anna Maria Calhoun, who had married Thomas Green Clemson in 1838. The Clemsons’ daughter, Floride Elizabeth, also inherited a portion. Tragically, Anna Calhoun Clemson did not take ownership of land until her two surviving children had already passed.
Anna Maria Calhoun Clemson willed her three-fourths share of Fort Hill to her husband, Thomas Clemson, with the caveat that he must die with a will. At Anna’s death in 1875, Thomas worked with two attorneys, James Rion and Richard Wright Simpson, to create his bequest that became Clemson University. If he had not, the granddaughter Floride Isabella Lee would have inherited the entire property in accordance with Anna Clemson’s will.

Through a succession of Calhoun-Clemson women, Fort Hill would come into Thomas Green Clemson’s possession. In 1888, Clemson bequeathed three-fourths of the Fort Hill plantation and $80,000 to the state of South Carolina for the establishment of a public scientific and agricultural college. He willed that Fort Hill “shall always be open for the inspection of visitors.”
Today, Fort Hill is just as Thomas Clemson envisioned — preserved, restored and open to the public for tours.
The enslaved African-Americans, whose story of resistance and resilience left little written records, built and operated from 1825 through 1865., Prior to Anna Clemson inheriting Fort Hill on January 21, 1872, Thomas Green Clemson began signing employment contracts in 1868 with former enslaved persons from Fort Hill and neighboring plantations.
**Freedman's Contracts**
Signed by Thomas Green Clemson
Life at Fort Hill, and all of its financial growth, was only possible because of the physical labor and sheer determination of the enslaved African Americans who toiled on the 450 acre cultivated land, producing maintaining the household, and performing construction of the plantation.
Since the enslaved who occupied Fort Hill left no written record, their perspective has been made virtually voiceless in history. In many cases, names and family connections are not known.
**African Americans at Fort Hill – Primary Documents**
1854 and 1865
Little is known about the families who were enslaved at Fort Hill by its three plantation era owners, John C. Calhoun, Floride Colhoun Calhoun, and Andrew Pickens Calhoun. There are records of a few family units, including: Sawney, his wife Tiller, and at least two of their children, Sawney Jr. and Issey; Daphne, her husband Bill Lawrence, and their children Susan Clemson Richardson and Benjamin; Sharper, his wife Caroline, and his daughter Tiller; and Nelly and her son Andy.

**Fort Hill**, also known as the **John C. Calhoun House and Library**, is a National Historic Landmark on the Clemson University campus in Pickens County, South Carolina, United States, near the City of Clemson.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_(Clemson_University,_South_Carolina)#cite_note-Censusmaps-4)
From 1825-1850, the house was the home of noted proponent of slavery and constitutional Nullification, John C. Calhoun, the 7th Vice President of the United States.

Clemson University was established on the Fort Hill slave-operated plantation site in 1889, and in accordance with the terms of its inheritance, has maintained the house and its immediate parcel as a museum and library — all that remains of what originally was an approximately 1,000 acre plantation estate.
Fort Hill
State historic marker for Fort Hill
The house was originally built as a four-room house about 1803 and was called **Clergy Hall** by Dr. James McElhenny, who was the pastor of Hopewell Presbyterian Church. The house later became the home of John C. Calhoun and his wife Floride Calhoun in 1825. Calhoun enlarged it to 14 rooms and renamed it Fort Hill for nearby Fort Rutledge, which was built around 1776. The architectural style is Greek Revival with Federal detailing and with simple interior detailing.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_(Clemson_University,_South_Carolina)#cite_note-5)
After John Calhoun's death in 1850, the property and the 50 slaves there passed to his wife to be shared with three of her children: Cornelia, John, and Anna Maria, wife of Thomas Green Clemson. Anna sold her share to Floride Calhoun. Floride Calhoun sold the plantation to her son, Andrew Pickens Calhoun, and held the mortgage. After Andrew died in 1865, she filed for foreclosure against Andrew's heirs before her death in 1866.
After lengthy legal proceedings, the plantation was auctioned at Walhalla in 1872. The executor of her estate won the auction, which was divided among her surviving heirs. Her daughter, Anna Clemson, received the residence with about 814 acres (329 ha) and her great-granddaughter, Floride Isabella Lee, received about 288 acres (117 ha). Thomas Green and Anna Clemson moved into Fort Hill in 1872. After Anna's death in 1875, Thomas Green Clemson inherited Fort Hill.

In his 1888 will, Clemson bequeathed more than 814 acres (329 ha) of the Fort Hill estate to the State of South Carolina for an agricultural college with a stipulation that the dwelling house "shall never be torn down or altered; but shall be kept in repair with all articles of furniture and vesture...and shall always be open for inspection of visitors."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_(Clemson_University,_South_Carolina)#cite_note-6)Clemson University has operated Fort Hill as a house museum as stipulated in the will. The house is all that remains of what was once an extensive plantation estate.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_(Clemson_University,_South_Carolina)#cite_note-scdahsum-7)
The home was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1960.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_(Clemson_University,_South_Carolina)#cite_note-nrhpinv2-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_(Clemson_University,_South_Carolina)#cite_note-nhlsum-3)
Fort Hill was closed for a two-year restoration project and was reopened in the spring of 2003. Fort Hill was named a national treasure by the [Save America's Treasures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Save_America's_Treasures "Save America's Treasures") program,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hill_(Clemson_University,_South_Carolina)#cite_note-8) and its artifacts are currently_[when?_] undergoing a comprehensive conservation program funded by this federal grant and matching funds.

### Contact Us

Facility Manager - Rollins Edwards Community Center [Email](mailto:bwest@summervillesc.gov) More Information
The Rollins Edwards Community Center opened on July 1, 2019. The 14,000 square foot building, located at 301 N. Hickory St., features a full-size gymnasium, three multipurpose rooms, a fitness room, a wellness center, and a catering kitchen. It is previously known as the S.C. National Guard Armory. It sat vacant for many years before the town bought the building in 2014. Rollins Edwards was a Dorchester County leader and World War II veteran who passed away in 2017.

# College of **Hospitality, Retail and Sport Management**
## Karen Edwards, J.D.
### Background
Karen Edwards serves as the College of HRSM's associate dean of academic programs and student affairs and is a senior instructor in the Department of Retailing at the University of South Carolina. Title: News Flash Archive - Former County Administrator Tommy Edwards passes away
