The original article was published from 11/11/2024 12:00:00 AM to 11/11/2026 11:59:00 PM
Thomas “Tommy” W. Edwards Jr., who served as Georgetown County Administrator from 1998 to 2008, died at Lowcountry Community Hospice House in Summerville on Nov. 9. He was 84.
Edwards was born on Aug. 15, 1940, in Marion. He was the son of the late Thomas W. Edwards Sr. and Octavia Edwards. He is remembered as a pillar of strength, service and commitment to his family and his community.
In high school, he was the captain of the basketball team, class President and President of the Beta Club. He graduated from Baptist College and received his master’s in Public Administration from Central Michigan University.
The decade Edwards spent leading Georgetown County capped off a 35-year career in local government. Within Georgetown County government, he is remembered as “a quiet, yet truly effective leader,” and as someone who was tough but fair, knew how to get things done, and a consummate professional. He was much more easygoing in his personal life and said at the time of his retirement that he was looking forward to being “a professional grandfather.” He loved fishing, golf, gardening, photography, and his dachshund, Maggie. He was counted as a friend by many.
During his time as Georgetown County Administrator, Edwards left his mark on the county. Among his most significant achievements, he spurred a group of community leaders to begin work on a long-range strategic plan for the county, which came to be known as Visions. The plan went through two phases, with the second being turned into an 18-year, $313.5 million capital improvement plan that built new libraries and community centers, parks, sports complexes, and other facilities that helped the county meet the demands of a growing population. The last project in the plan was just completed earlier this year.
During his tenure, Edwards was also responsible for consolidating county departments, establishing the county’s stormwater department, and strengthening financial controls. “When Edwards took over as Administrator, no provisions were being made for the future financially or technologically,” recalled Dwight McInvaill, Georgetown County Library Director.

“The county was behind,” McInvaill said. “There were a handful of computers at most. He turned things around and established a good foundation to allow the county to grow and prosper.”
Edwards launched the Georgetown County Efficiency and Effectiveness initiative, which produced a report in 2004 that included 67 major recommendations from technological improvements to solid-waste operations, with a goal of saving $850,000 in the first year and $5 million over five years. Notably, Georgetown County was also named a National Civic League All-America County in 2004 under Edwards’ leadership.
After his retirement, Edwards served on the Georgetown County Planning Commission from 2008-2011 and remained a resident on the Waccamaw Neck. Due to his significant contributions to the county, the Georgetown County Airport Terminal was named in Edwards’ honor upon its completion in early 2009. That facility was also part of the Visions Plan.
“The Georgetown County team is deeply saddened to learn of Mr. Edwards’ passing,” said Georgetown County spokeswoman Jackie Broach. “Mr. Edwards dedicated his life to the service of South Carolina’s residents. His vision and leadership were transformative, driving major advancements in technology, citizen engagement, and strategic planning initiatives in Georgetown County. Under his leadership, the county achieved many milestones, including the Visions I and Vision II initiatives. We honor his legacy of innovation, efficiency, and community-focused service and extend our deepest condolences to his family, friends, and all who were touched by his dedicated service to our community.”
Edwards began his career in government in the early 1970s and over the years served as Director of Administration for the City of North Charleston, and City Manager in Newberry and Florence. In his last post before coming to Georgetown County, he was Florence County Administrator.
Among many honors throughout this lifetime, Edwards was awarded the Order of the Palmetto, the most distinguished civilian award granted by the State, in recognition of his contributions to his community and local government. He was also named a Paul Harris Fellow for his service to the Rotary Club and received a Key to the City of Florence in 1995. He was a life member of the South Carolina City-County Managers Association, and through the years served as its director, secretary, treasurer, vice president, and president.

Edwards is survived by his wife, Linda Fulton Edwards of Georgetown; children Stephanie Hall (Stan), Thomas W. Edwards III (Grace) and Karen Edwards (Rob) of Charleston, and Brian Edwards (Jennie) of Florence; and 10 grandchildren. In lieu of flowers, contributions may be made to the Charleston Animal Society.

# College of **Hospitality, Retail and Sport Management**
## Karen Edwards, J.D.
### Background
Karen Edwards serves as the College of HRSM's associate dean of academic programs and student affairs and is a senior instructor in the Department of Retailing at the University of South Carolina. Recipient of the University’s 2019 Garnet Apple Award for Teaching Innovation, the 2017 Faculty Integrity Award, and the 2010-11 Harry E. Varney Distinguished Teacher of the Year Award, Edwards teaches in the areas of digital commerce, asset protection and law-related issues affecting retailers. Edwards has developed numerous undergraduate and graduate-level courses, such as Law for Retailers, Fashion and the Law and Asset Protection for Retailers. She has also led numerous study abroad programs and co-developed the University’s first-ever virtual study abroad course. In 2016, Edwards received the Brian J. and Linda L. Mihalik Global Scholar Award. She is a frequent presenter and past associate director for distributed learning at the University’s Center for Teaching Excellence (CTE).
Edwards’ research focuses on legal issues affecting retailers/service providers and best practices in online learning. In 2019, she was named a Fulbright Specialist through the U.S. State Department. She was elected to the Loss Prevention Foundation (LPF) board of directors in 2022. Edwards' research has been published in International Journal of Retail and Distribution Management, Journal of Retail and Consumer Services, Tourism Management, Sport Marketing Quarterly, and other scholarly publications. Her work has been presented at various conferences, including the University of Queensland Digital Service Transformation Summit, Quality Matters annual conference, the Association of Marketing Theory and Practice, and Online Learning Consortium Accelerate. She is a reviewer for Journal of Business Research, Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services, Journal of Services Marketing, and Bloomsbury/Fairchild Publishing.

## Karen Edwards, J.D.
### Background
Prior to arriving at USC, Edwards practiced law with Duff, White and Turner, L.L.C., a firm serving public school districts and colleges across South Carolina. Her practice, which focused on employment law and education law, included significant amounts of workforce training on legal matters for her clients. Before attending law school, Edwards worked for a number of years in retail management, including roles as a merchandise coordinator, human resources manager and corporate trainer. She earned her Juris Doctor degree from the Joseph F. Rice School of Law and her bachelor's degree from Coker University in Hartsville, South Carolina. Edwards is a past chair of Coker's Board of Trustees, and a member of the South Carolina Bar Association, South Carolina Women in Higher Education, American Collegiate Retailing Association and American MENSA.

Title: News Flash Archive - Former County Administrator Tommy Edwards passes away
Chunks: 0,1,2
The original article was published from 11/11/2024 12:00:00 AM to 11/11/2026 11:59:00 PM
Thomas “Tommy” W. Edwards Jr., who served as Georgetown County Administrator from 1998 to 2008, died at Lowcountry Community Hospice House in Summerville on Nov. 9. He was 84.
Edwards was born on Aug. 15, 1940, in Marion. He was the son of the late Thomas W. Edwards Sr. and Octavia Edwards. He is remembered as a pillar of strength, service and commitment to his family and his community.
In high school, he was the captain of the basketball team, class President and President of the Beta Club. He graduated from Baptist College and received his master’s in Public Administration from Central Michigan University.
The decade Edwards spent leading Georgetown County capped off a 35-year career in local government. Within Georgetown County government, he is remembered as “a quiet, yet truly effective leader,” and as someone who was tough but fair, knew how to get things done, and a consummate professional. He was much more easygoing in his personal life and said at the time of his retirement that he was looking forward to being “a professional grandfather.” He loved fishing, golf, gardening, photography, and his dachshund, Maggie. He was counted as a friend by many.
During his time as Georgetown County Administrator, Edwards left his mark on the county. Among his most significant achievements, he spurred a group of community leaders to begin work on a long-range strategic plan for the county, which came to be known as Visions. The plan went through two phases, with the second being turned into an 18-year, $313.5 million capital improvement plan that built new libraries and community centers, parks, sports complexes, and other facilities that helped the county meet the demands of a growing population. The last project in the plan was just completed earlier this year.
During his tenure, Edwards was also responsible for consolidating county departments, establishing the county’s stormwater department, and strengthening financial controls. “When Edwards took over as Administrator, no provisions were being made for the future financially or technologically,” recalled Dwight McInvaill, Georgetown County Library Director.

“The county was behind,” McInvaill said. “There were a handful of computers at most. He turned things around and established a good foundation to allow the county to grow and prosper.”
Edwards launched the Georgetown County Efficiency and Effectiveness initiative, which produced a report in 2004 that included 67 major recommendations from technological improvements to solid-waste operations, with a goal of saving $850,000 in the first year and $5 million over five years. Notably, Georgetown County was also named a National Civic League All-America County in 2004 under Edwards’ leadership.
After his retirement, Edwards served on the Georgetown County Planning Commission from 2008-2011 and remained a resident on the Waccamaw Neck. Due to his significant contributions to the county, the Georgetown County Airport Terminal was named in Edwards’ honor upon its completion in early 2009. That facility was also part of the Visions Plan.
“The Georgetown County team is deeply saddened to learn of Mr. Edwards’ passing,” said Georgetown County spokeswoman Jackie Broach. “Mr. Edwards dedicated his life to the service of South Carolina’s residents. His vision and leadership were transformative, driving major advancements in technology, citizen engagement, and strategic planning initiatives in Georgetown County. Under his leadership, the county achieved many milestones, including the Visions I and Vision II initiatives. We honor his legacy of innovation, efficiency, and community-focused service and extend our deepest condolences to his family, friends, and all who were touched by his dedicated service to our community.”
Edwards began his career in government in the early 1970s and over the years served as Director of Administration for the City of North Charleston, and City Manager in Newberry and Florence. In his last post before coming to Georgetown County, he was Florence County Administrator.
Among many honors throughout this lifetime, Edwards was awarded the Order of the Palmetto, the most distinguished civilian award granted by the State, in recognition of his contributions to his community and local government. He was also named a Paul Harris Fellow for his service to the Rotary Club and received a Key to the City of Florence in 1995. He was a life member of the South Carolina City-County Managers Association, and through the years served as its director, secretary, treasurer, vice president, and president.

Edwards is survived by his wife, Linda Fulton Edwards of Georgetown; children Stephanie Hall (Stan), Thomas W. Edwards III (Grace) and Karen Edwards (Rob) of Charleston, and Brian Edwards (Jennie) of Florence; and 10 grandchildren. In lieu of flowers, contributions may be made to the Charleston Animal Society.

## Fort Hill State Girls Volleyball Champion, 2013
Collection Name
About
Body
Fort Hill High School State Girls Volleyball Champions, 2013
On November 16, 2013, Fort Hill became the second Allegany County high school to capture the Maryland State Women's Volleyball Championship. Fort Hill completed a perfect undefeated 19-0 season in College Park by defeating a school from Baltimore County for the 1A title.
Subject

## Fort Hill High State Softball Champions, 2008
Collection Name
About
Body
In 2008, Fort Hill High School won the Maryland Class 1A State Girls Softball Championship. The team members as depicted in this photograph are as follows:
First row, left to right - Brittany Hines, Lauren Fansler, Adria Lewis, Destiny James, Becca Valentine
Second row - Alyssa Yost, Olivia Stanley, Cierra Miller, Lindsey Fisher, Shari Beavers, Alex Schupfer, Kathryn Huber, Brittany Whiteman, Acacia Squires
Subject

## First girls' basketball game
Collection Name
About
Body
The first known girls' basketball game to take place in Allegany County occurred on the afternoon of March 1, 1910. This was an exhibition game between the Blues and the Whites which was played in the basement of Allegany County High School. The girls wore white middies, very full black bloomers, fastened well below the knees, and black cotton stockings. One basket was used during the game which was won by the Whites by a score of 27-25. A girls' athletic association was formed during that same year.
From: "The Golden Jubilee Magazine of Allegany High School, 1889 -1938"
Subject

## Crystal Fields
Collection Name
About
Body
On July 17, 1979 eleven year old Crystal Fields of Cumberland won the national championship in her division in the National Pitch-Hit-Run Competition which was held in Seattle, Washington. A reception in her honor was held later in the week by the Mayor and City Council of Cumberland where Crystal received the, “Key to the City of Cumberland”.
Subject

## Mary Eversole, 1949-2015
Collection Name
About
Body
Allegany County resident, Mary Eversole, was the 2006 Maryland State Class A Horseshoe Women’s Champion. She also won this title seven of the last eight years. In 1999, over a period of three days in 95-degree weather, Mary competed against 45 other women in the World Horseshoe Tournament and was a Bronze Medalist.
In her own words, Mary says, “I really enjoy the game. It’s not something I feel I have to do, but something I do because it’s fun. That’s the key to winning.”
Subject

## Marie Boyd Eichler, 1905-1991
Collection Name
About
Body
Marie Boyd Eichler
It was February 25, 1924 and the six-girl basketball team of Lonaconing Central High School was going up against Ursuline Academy of Cumberland. Lonaconing would go on to win by the lop-sided score of 163 to 3.
Central’s Marie Boyd would go into the
Guinness Book of World Records  
for scoring 156 points in the game. She is still listed first in the National High School Sports Record Book for most points scored and field goals made (77) in a single six-girl basketball game.
Subject

## Cumberland Heat
Collection Name
About
Body
The Cumberland Heat
In 1996 the United States Specialty Sports Association (USSSA) authorized women’s fast-pitch softball. It was immediately established in Maryland, and the Cumberland Heat was founded.
Subject

## Central High School basketball team, 1920s
Collection Name
About
Body
The Central High School girls basketball team of Lonaconing holds the Allegany County basketball record for consecutive wins having won 65 games in a row. This was over the course of three seasons; 1922, 1923, and 1924.
Central’s winning streak was snapped by Beall High School in 1924 when they were defeated by a score of 36 to 35 in a Western Maryland Interscholastic League (WMIL) championship playoff game. The WMIL was, at one time, the oldest continuous high school athletic league in the country.
Subject

## Betty Hodges, Jean Arendes Bibby, and Evelyn Bowie
Collection Name
About
Body
Betty Hodges, Jean Arendes Bibby, and Evelyn Bowie
The Cumberland Country Club (CCC) was established in 1919. The first woman to win the Women's Club Championship was Bess Shearer in 1922. For the next five decades, with the exception of 1943-1947 when no tournaments were held, the above three women were felt to have dominated the golfing scene at the Cumberland Country Club, as well as throughout the area. As noted below, and in addition to golf, they also made their presence known in skiing and tennis.
Subject

## Jean Arendes Bibby, 1908 - 1995
Collection Name
About
Body
Jean Bibby was known as “Miss Golf” in Cumberland and is considered the greatest woman golfer in Allegany County history. Between the years 1925 and 1976 Jean Bibby won a total of twenty Cumberland Country Club golf championships, in 1924, 1925, 1926, 1927, 1928, 1929, 1931, 1932, 1935, 1936, 1937, 1951, 1952, 1953, 1957, 1960, 1968, 1971, 1975, and 1976.
Subject

Post season awards I have earned include All City, All Area, and All AMAC conference. Following tradition, the coaches of the football, baseball, basketball, and soccer teams voted and I was chosen for the prestigious award of Most Outstanding Male Junior Athlete. # Fort Hill seeks region title at Northern
*   Story by Cumberland Times News, Md.      
*   Fort Hill seeks region title at Northern
Alex McGinley, Cumberland Times-News, Md.·Cumberland Times News, Md.
Wed, November 11, 2026 at 11:16 PM UTC·
2 min read
ACCIDENT — Even after losing to Northern Garrett twice in the regular season, Fort Hill is confident it can turn things around in its third meeting.
No. 2 Fort Hill and No. 1 Northern will meet for the Class 1A West Region I championship on Wednesday at 6 p.m. in Accident.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
The winner of Wednesday's match will move on to the state quarterfinals this weekend.
Northern (17-5) defeated Fort Hill (13-4) 3-0 (25-23, 25-21, 25-14) in the Sentinels' second match of the season on Sept. 14 in Accident.
After starting the season 0-2, the Sentinels won 10 of their next 11 matches. Their only loss in that span was to Northern on Sept. 29 in Cumberland.
But the Sentinels played much better the second time around against the Huskies in a match that went to four sets.
Fort Hill led 24-23 in the first set before Northern claimed three points in a row to win the first set.
The Sentinels then earned the second set 25-19 before the Huskies closed the match with two sets of 25-17.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
"It's always hard playing away, and it's definitely hard playing out there," Fort Hill coach Jordan Fradiska said after his team's win over Mountain Ridge on Friday. "Obviously, they beat a good team in Clear Spring. We took a set from them this year. Obviously, there's no moral victories."
Fort Hill is coming off a sweep over No. 3 Mountain Ridge in the semifinals. The Sentinels needed five sets twice to beat the Miners in the regular season.

# Fort Hill seeks region title at Northern
The Sentinels' only two losses in Western Maryland Athletic Conference play came to the Huskies. Fort Hill's other two losses came to non-conference opponents in North Hagerstown and Hampshire — both of those matches went to five sets.
Aside from their four losses and the two regular-season matches to Mountain Ridge, the Sentinels have dropped just one set.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Fort Hill is seeking its second region title and first since its state-championship winning team in 2013.
"I think if we come together and play like we did tonight with the energy we had, I think we'll do just fine," senior captain Tatum Bishop said.
"We've grown a lot as a team together. We are all friends outside of here, so I think we have good chemistry as a team."
Northern is coming off a 3-1 victory over No. 5 Clear Spring in the semifinals in a rematch of last year's region final. The Blazers, who won the state championship last season, claimed the first set 26-24 before the Huskies earned the next three sets.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
The Huskies finished undefeated in West MAC play, and all five of their losses came in a tournament in Hedgesville.
Northern is seeking just its second region title and first since winning the state championship in 1985.

Title: Fort Hill lineman Carter Hess wins Player of the Year
Chunks: 0,1,2
Mar. 29—CUMBERLAND — For just the second time in the 50-year history of the award, a lineman has won area Player of the Year.
Carter Hess, standing at 6-foot-2, 295 pounds, kept opposing head coaches up at night over the past three seasons, and he'll likely keep them up in college too, playing for Division 1 Fordham University next fall.
Advertisement
It was unsurprising then, that Hess was the runaway pick for the area's top player by those same coaches.
The right tackle and interior defensive line standout will receive the award at the 75th Dick Sterne Memorial Dapper Dan Sports Banquet on Sunday, April 28, at 4 p.m. in the Ali Ghan Shrine Club Ballroom.
"I would venture to say he's one of the best players to ever play at Fort Hill," his head coach Zack Alkire said. "The more that we asked Carter to do, the better he'd get at it."
Hess received all but two Player of the Year votes, with the other two going to Will Patterson, who shared Offensive Player of the Year honors with Sentinel back Jabril Daniels on Thursday.
Advertisement
The Fort Hill lineman has won an award in every full varsity football season he's played. Hess was area Defensive Player of the Year last year and Lineman of the Year in 2021.
The rest of the state finally realized Hess' dominance this year, something this area's head coaches were already painfully aware of.
He was the recipient of Class 1A state Player of the Year by the Maryland Football Foundation and MPSSAA Defensive Player of the Year, regardless of class, by Baltimore Sports and Life.
It was fitting, then, that Hess ended a 24-year drought since the last time a lineman was this area's Player of the Year, achieving the feat only Moorefield's Justin Williams, who went on to play at West Virginia University, did in 1999.
Advertisement
At the time, Williams was the first lineman in West Virginia scholastic football history to start on four state championship-winning teams.
Hess never got that chance because his freshman year was shorted by the COVID-19 pandemic, but he did star on three Maryland Class 1A champions, and Fort Hill was 38-1 over that span.

While Hess' strength is well-documented, Alkire highlighted his technique and preparation as things that set the senior apart.
"People think about how strong he is, but he has great feet, hands and quickness," Alkire said. "He sees the field well, and that's because of his intelligence. He's always in the right spot because he studies.
Advertisement
"You can see how much film everybody watches, and every day he's the leader, watching 3-4 hours more than the next kid."
Hess finished his final campaign in red and white as the area's leading tackler for a second straight year, racking up 145 of them (74 solos) to go along with an area-best 13 sacks, 23 tackles for loss and four forced fumbles.
For the under-recruited Hess, who would've played Power 5 football if he was three inches taller, it all began in the weight room.
"He's a very self-motivated player. He worked his tail off," said Alkire. "He had to work harder than everybody else because all eyes were on him. Even though he was self-motivated, he expected the same out of everybody else.
Advertisement
"Most of the guys aren't going to work as hard as him, but he expected his teammates to approach that level. He never took plays off, even in practice. When they weren't giving him their best, he'd let them know and when Carter Hess spoke, people listened."
It was difficult for Hess to go 100% in practice all year out of fear that he might injure the players going against him.
Fort Hill had no junior linemen in its program in 2023, prompting Fort Hill to call up a collection of sophomores to groom them for the starting role next year.
"Carter's biggest obstacle is he had put himself in a position where unless we would take one of our starters out, it was difficult for him as the season moved forward to work as hard in practice," Alkire said.
Advertisement
"He was going against much younger, smaller kids in practice. As the season progressed, he found that middle ground again where he could push himself without taking it too far. ... By doing that, he made the whole team better."

Hess' work ethic was instilled by his father, Sam Hess, who still holds the state record for rushing yards in a game after he ran for 446 yards as Hancock's star running back against St. James in 1998.
Carter is now the third person in his immediate family to earn a collegiate sports scholarship. His father went on to play at Shepherd University, and his sister, Chloe Hess, is in her sophomore year as the ace of Lehigh's softball team — she was second-team All-Patriot League as a freshman.
Carter Hess won state championships at Fort Hill across three sports.
Advertisement
Hess became Fort Hill's first individual wrestling state champion since Dave Phillips took home the 189-pound state title in 1990 when he won the 285-pound Class 2A/1A championship this winter to complete an unbeaten 33-0 season.
Hess is also the two-time defending Maryland Class 1A discus state champion, setting a state record last spring with a 168-foot heave.
Coaches in the Western Maryland Athletic Conference can now breathe a sigh of relief because Hess is the Patriot League's problem.
And there's little doubt in Alkire's mind that his prized lineman will be a problem at the next level.
Advertisement
"I think him going to Fordham, he'll see the field sooner rather than later," Alkire said. "It's a good situation. He's going to be the hardest worker in the room. I believe he's going to make his presence felt Day 1 and earn some playing time as a freshman. He's going to be a very good player in that league."
Alex Rychwalski is a sports reporter at the Cumberland Times-News. Follow him on Twitter @arychwal.

Title: GLORY AT GREENWAY | Allegany-Fort Hill hits 90th anniversary - CNHI
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6
October 30, 2026 by
CUMBERLAND — A tradition that has lasted 90 years and counting isn’t the only thing Cumberland got from the inaugural meeting between Allegany and Fort Hill on Thanksgiving Day in 1936.
The game, which Allegany won, 19-17, featured two head coaches — Herman Ball and John J. “Bobby” Cavanaugh — who had remarkable legacies beyond the Cumberland gridiron.
On one side at Community Park was Herman Ball, who was putting the finishing touches on a 9-0-1 season in his inaugural campaign as Allegany’s head ball coach.
Ball, an Elkins, West Virginia, native, attended Davis & Elkins College and played at guard on the 1933 team that led all of college football in points scored with 345. Ball played under Cam Henderson, who was featured in Ripley’s Believe It or Not in 1933 for coaching all sports at Davis & Elkins without assistants, trainers or scouts.
Following his time at Davis & Elkins, Ball was hired as head coach at Ridgeley in 1935, finishing 3-3-1 before crossing the Potomac to take the same post at Allegany.
Ball not only won the first Turkey Day game between Allegany and Fort Hill, but he also was the first of five Allegany head coaches to win their first Turkey Day/Homecoming game against Fort Hill.
Bill Bowers, in his second stint as Allegany head coach, won in 1943, 14-7. George Stimmel won The Snow Game in 1971, 18-14. Jack Gilmore shut out the Sentinels in 1985, 24-0. Tim Foley, serving as interim head coach while Tom Preaskorn was in Iraq as a major in the West Virginia Army National Guard, won the 2007 matchup, 33-14.
Ball coached the Campers for seven seasons and was 6-1 against the Sentinels, with the lone loss a 20-0 defeat in 1940.

After his opening campaign, Ball’s next three Allegany squads had three straight 8-2 seasons — outside of a 20-0 loss to Waynesburg (Pennsylvania) in 1937, the Campers lost by no more than seven points during those three seasons.
Ball’s 1940 season finished 3-7, thanks in large part to injuries piled on top of a host of graduates from the 1939 team, including future NFLers Tommy Mont and Jim Gaffney.
The Campers in 1941 capped off their first unblemished season in school history with a 19-0 romp over Fort Hill on Turkey Day for a 9-0 finish.
The West Siders were again victorious in 1942’s Turkey Day affair, a 17-6 win over the Sentinels to seal a second straight undefeated season at 8-0.
Part of Allegany’s success in ‘41 and ‘42 was due to Ball implementing the T-formation that was sweeping the nation thanks in large part to the Chicago Bears, coached by the legendary George Halas, and Clark Shaughnessy, who left Stanford after the 1941 season amid fears that the university was going to cut the football program due to the war.
Following his departure from Stanford, Shaughnessy signed a “lifetime contract” at Maryland. With the Terps, Shaughnessy installed a pass-oriented version of the T-formation, leading to Mont, Maryland’s starting quarterback, being named an honorable mention All-American and the No. 3 passer in the country.
Ball’s reign as Allegany’s football coach came to an abrupt end in February 1943 when he submitted his resignation due to an “ignored” salary increase request.
“I first conferred with Charles L. Kopp, superintendent of schools, on July 1, 1942, relative to an increase in my salary of $1,980 for serving as football coach, a member of the teaching staff and assistant principal,” Ball said in the Feb. 8, 1943, edition of The Cumberland News.
“Since that time on several occasions, I have talked to Superintendent Kopp and two members of the board in connection with my request, and in each instance, I was advised that the matter would be settled at the next meeting.

“A number of meetings of the board have been held since July of last year, and so far Superintendent Kopp and the board members have not even extended to me the courtesy of a reply containing their refusal or approval.”
Ball’s time with the Campers ended with a record of 54-13-1.
“It is with great regret that I leave Allegany,” Ball said in the same interview. “I’ve had many happy associations there and I would not be leaving except that I feel that I’ve been ignored in my efforts to secure an adjustment in salary.”
Ball’s resignation sparked mass outrage, especially among the Allegany student body.
Nearly 40% of the school’s 1,525 students participated in a walkout on Feb. 9, 1943. The students paraded past the Board of Education offices on Washington Street and then marched to Fort Hill High School, where the group of 607 picked up approximately 100 sympathetic Sentinels to join their cause.
Despite Ball’s insistence that the students not take action on his behalf, the group descended upon Baltimore Street with chants of “We Want Ball,” No Coach, No School” and even some chants against the school’s administration.
Ball’s resignation was accepted by the Board of Education on Feb. 12, 1943.
A move to College Park
On July 8, 1943, two days before the Allied forces launched Operation Husky — a massive amphibious and airborne invasion of the Italian island of Sicily — Ball was hired by the University of Maryland to assist in its physical fitness training program for approximately 1,100 Army trainees.
Clarence “Doc” Spears said that if Maryland was to have a football team in the fall, Ball would be on his staff. Spears took over as head coach of the Maryland football team when Shaughnessy left the Terps after just one year to lead the football program at Pitt.
The Terps did have football that fall, with just one player with collegiate varsity experience answering Spears’ call for help.
Of the nearly 400 male students at Maryland who showed interest in playing football that fall — the Army trainees were not eligible — Spears and his staff whittled it down to around 50.

Many of the players had no high school football experience, let alone game time at any collegiate level, so the first day of practice was spent doing the fundamentals: passing, kicking, snapping and tackling.
Spears, Ball and Co. finished 4-5 that year, with a 2-0 mark in Southeastern Conference play with wins over Wake Forest and VMI.
Back in Cumberland, Bowers took over as Allegany head coach for the second time, with this stint spanning three seasons.
After a 5-4 mark in 1943, Bowers and the Campers went 9-1 and 8-0-1 before Bob Pence took over in 1946.
Ball remained on the Maryland staff for the 1944 season, when the Terps finished 1-7-1 with a season-concluding 8-6 victory over VMI.
In August of 1945, following Spears’ resignation, Maryland president H.C. Byrd denied reports that Ball had been named head coach.
The school ultimately hired the legendary Bear Bryant, who went 6-2-1 in his lone season in College Park before leaving for Kentucky, in part due to his tumultuous relationship with Byrd.
Ball, however, continued his ascent up the football ladder in 1945.
Still a member of Bryant’s staff at Maryland, Ball was appointed as a part-time scout with the Washington Redskins in August 1945.
In the Dec. 27, 1945, edition of the Cumberland Evening Times, it was reported that the Redskins were pursuing a trade for Mont to join Gaffney, who was drafted by the Redskins in 1944.
The deal would send Frankie Filchock to the New York Giants for Mont and Paul Stenn, with Mont joining the Redskins upon his discharge from the military. Mont was serving in the Army and stationed in Germany.
A slightly altered trade went through a few weeks later, with the Redskins shipping Filchock to New York in exchange for Stenn and a player to be named later.
Following his military service, Mont — and Shaughnessy — returned to Maryland in 1946. Mont was joined by two Cumberlanders on the team in Fort Hill’s Fred Davis and LaSalle’s Norman Geatz.

In May 1947, Mont, the player to be named later in the trade a year prior with the Giants, signed a contract with the Redskins.
In 1946, Ball stepped down from his post as an assistant at Maryland to join the Redskins in a full-time capacity as scout.
Head man for the Redskins
The departure from Maryland lasted only months, as it was announced in September that Ball was rejoining the Maryland coaching staff in an undisclosed, but presumably minor, role.
Ball remained with the Redskins and, in 1949, was appointed as the team’s line coach under new head coach John Whelchel.
There were widespread reports in Washington of coaching departures, including Ball, following a 49-14 thrashing at the hands of the Eagles on Oct. 23, 1949.
Two weeks later, Whelchel was fired after a 3-3-1 start to the year.
Ball, 39 years old at the time, was named head coach — the Redskins went 1-4 the rest of the way, notching a 30-0 win over the Packers in the second-to-last game of the season.
Although Ball wasn’t officially given an interim tag, Washington owner George Preston Marshall reiterated in January 1950 that Ball would remain as head coach for the upcoming season.
After an undefeated preseason and 38-14 win over the Baltimore Colts in the season opener, the Redskins lost seven straight and finished 3-9.
Ball and the Redskins got off to an 0-3 start to the 1951 campaign, and Ball was fired as a result on Oct. 18.
The decision led to a bizarre situation as it was widely reported that Bears assistant Hunk Anderson would be the new head coach. Anderson was prevented from starting his new post due to contract issues with Chicago’s George Halas and, after Marshall refused to provide the Bears with compensation, Ball’s assistant Dick Todd was named interim head coach.
Ball returned to his old post as chief scout before resigning on Dec. 17, 1954, after briefly returning to the Washington sidelines as an assistant.
Weeks after his resignation, Ball was hired as an assistant with the Pittsburgh Steelers.

Ball’s tenure in the Steel City lasted one season, taking a job as a line coach and scout with the Baltimore Colts on Feb. 2, 1956.
Ball stayed with the Colts for seven years, capturing back-to-back NFL titles in 1958 and 1959.
Ball was dismissed after the 1962 season when Colts head coach Weeb Ewbank was replaced by Don Shula.
Ball left the NFL for the AFL’s Buffalo Bills, which was a short-lived stint, as he returned to the NFL a year later when former Redskins coach Joe Kuharich was hired by the Philadelphia Eagles.
Kuharich and his staff were fired after a 2-12 finish in 1968, but Ball stayed in Philadelphia as the team’s director of player personnel.
In 1977, Ball announced his retirement after a career that spanned 34 years in the NFL. He stayed with the Eagles in an advisory role until 1986.
“Herman is one of the distinguished gentlemen in the NFL,” said then-Eagles coach Dick Vermeil. “We all have a great deal of admiration and respect for him and feel very fortunate that he has agreed to remain close to the organization in an advisory capacity.”
In 1985, Ball was inducted into the Allegany Hall of Fame.
Fourteen years later, on Jan. 12, 1999, Ball died at the age of 88.
Cavanaugh’s influence on city sports
While Ball’s legacy mostly spanned the professional ranks, Cavanaugh left a lasting impact on Cumberland and Allegany County.
A native New Englander, Cavanaugh played football, basketball, baseball and ice hockey at Crosby High School in Waterbury, Connecticut.
Cumberland wasn’t on his radar until his graduation from Washington College on Maryland’s Eastern Shore when Cavanaugh heard that Penn Avenue was seeking someone to coach “all types of sports.”
From 1928, when he was hired, until 1935, when Penn Avenue closed its high school program, Cavanaugh coached six sports: basketball, soccer, baseball, track, swimming and football. He even taught tumbling at one time.

Cavanaugh was the referee in the first Thanksgiving Day football game played between city rivals when Allegany obliterated LaSalle, 59-0, at Mid-City Park in 1928.
When Penn Avenue decided to start its football program in the fall of 1932, Cavanaugh inherited the football job as a one-man coaching staff.
In 1935, Cavanaugh’s Maroons won the City championship, beating LaSalle, 24-0, and Allegany, 20-6, and finished 7-1-1.
Cavanaugh’s Penn Avenue squads went 11-12-8 in four seasons.
Losses bookended Cavanaugh’s first and only season as Fort Hill football head coach — the Sentinels fell to Windber, Pennsylvania, 56-6, in the season opener before losing to Allegany in the first Turkey Day game between the Campers and Sentinels.
Fort Hill finished its inaugural season 6-2 and Johnny Long became head coach in 1937, lightening Cavanaugh’s load and allowing him to coach basketball and baseball.
Cavanaugh’s legacy on the hardwood spanned 30 years between Fort Hill and Penn Avenue between 1929 and 1958, compiling a record of 525-216 with seven state championships.
Four of Cavanaugh’s state championships came during the pre-Maryland Public Secondary Schools Athletic Association era, when Cumberland schools won 12 of the 13 state championships between 1927 and 1939.

Title: Fort Hill: National Historic Landmark
Chunks: 0,1
Prior to the Revolutionary War, the Cherokee called the land Esseneca. William Bartram visited this Lower Town twice, writing that it “is a respectable settlement, situated on the East Bank of the Keowee river.”
Before Fort Hill, the antebellum plantation of John C. Calhoun, South Carolina’s pre-eminent 19th century statesman, there was four-room Clergy Hall. Originally built in 1803, Clergy Hall served as the manse or parsonage for nearby Hopewell-Keowee Church, now known as Old Stone Presbyterian Church. Next, Floride Bonneau Colhoun, John C. Calhoun’s mother-in-law, purchased the 600 acre property; U.S. Vice President Calhoun’s family called the expanded structure Fort Hill, starting in 1830, after Revolutionary War Fort Rutledge.
In total, ten rooms were added to the structure and additional acreage was purchased by John C. Calhoun; however, he was not the owner until 1836, after the death of his mother-in-law.When John C. died in 1850, his wife Floride became the sole owner of the Fort Hill home and 1,341 acres of land. When she passed in 1866, portions of the property then went to their daughter and sole surviving child, Anna Maria Calhoun, who had married Thomas Green Clemson in 1838. The Clemsons’ daughter, Floride Elizabeth, also inherited a portion. Tragically, Anna Calhoun Clemson did not take ownership of land until her two surviving children had already passed.
Anna Maria Calhoun Clemson willed her three-fourths share of Fort Hill to her husband, Thomas Clemson, with the caveat that he must die with a will. At Anna’s death in 1875, Thomas worked with two attorneys, James Rion and Richard Wright Simpson, to create his bequest that became Clemson University. If he had not, the granddaughter Floride Isabella Lee would have inherited the entire property in accordance with Anna Clemson’s will.

Through a succession of Calhoun-Clemson women, Fort Hill would come into Thomas Green Clemson’s possession. In 1888, Clemson bequeathed three-fourths of the Fort Hill plantation and $80,000 to the state of South Carolina for the establishment of a public scientific and agricultural college. He willed that Fort Hill “shall always be open for the inspection of visitors.”
Today, Fort Hill is just as Thomas Clemson envisioned — preserved, restored and open to the public for tours.
The enslaved African-Americans, whose story of resistance and resilience left little written records, built and operated from 1825 through 1865., Prior to Anna Clemson inheriting Fort Hill on January 21, 1872, Thomas Green Clemson began signing employment contracts in 1868 with former enslaved persons from Fort Hill and neighboring plantations.
**Freedman's Contracts**
Signed by Thomas Green Clemson
Life at Fort Hill, and all of its financial growth, was only possible because of the physical labor and sheer determination of the enslaved African Americans who toiled on the 450 acre cultivated land, producing maintaining the household, and performing construction of the plantation.
Since the enslaved who occupied Fort Hill left no written record, their perspective has been made virtually voiceless in history. In many cases, names and family connections are not known.
**African Americans at Fort Hill – Primary Documents**
1854 and 1865
Little is known about the families who were enslaved at Fort Hill by its three plantation era owners, John C. Calhoun, Floride Colhoun Calhoun, and Andrew Pickens Calhoun. There are records of a few family units, including: Sawney, his wife Tiller, and at least two of their children, Sawney Jr. and Issey; Daphne, her husband Bill Lawrence, and their children Susan Clemson Richardson and Benjamin; Sharper, his wife Caroline, and his daughter Tiller; and Nelly and her son Andy.
Read more about African Americans at Fort Hill.

October 30, 2026 by
CUMBERLAND — A tradition that has lasted 90 years and counting isn’t the only thing Cumberland got from the inaugural meeting between Allegany and Fort Hill on Thanksgiving Day in 1936.
The game, which Allegany won, 19-17, featured two head coaches — Herman Ball and John J. “Bobby” Cavanaugh — who had remarkable legacies beyond the Cumberland gridiron.
On one side at Community Park was Herman Ball, who was putting the finishing touches on a 9-0-1 season in his inaugural campaign as Allegany’s head ball coach.
Ball, an Elkins, West Virginia, native, attended Davis & Elkins College and played at guard on the 1933 team that led all of college football in points scored with 345. Ball played under Cam Henderson, who was featured in Ripley’s Believe It or Not in 1933 for coaching all sports at Davis & Elkins without assistants, trainers or scouts.
Following his time at Davis & Elkins, Ball was hired as head coach at Ridgeley in 1935, finishing 3-3-1 before crossing the Potomac to take the same post at Allegany.
Ball not only won the first Turkey Day game between Allegany and Fort Hill, but he also was the first of five Allegany head coaches to win their first Turkey Day/Homecoming game against Fort Hill.
Bill Bowers, in his second stint as Allegany head coach, won in 1943, 14-7. George Stimmel won The Snow Game in 1971, 18-14. Jack Gilmore shut out the Sentinels in 1985, 24-0. Tim Foley, serving as interim head coach while Tom Preaskorn was in Iraq as a major in the West Virginia Army National Guard, won the 2007 matchup, 33-14.
Ball coached the Campers for seven seasons and was 6-1 against the Sentinels, with the lone loss a 20-0 defeat in 1940.
texts.1:
After his opening campaign, Ball’s next three Allegany squads had three straight 8-2 seasons — outside of a 20-0 loss to Waynesburg (Pennsylvania) in 1937, the Campers lost by no more than seven points during those three seasons.
Ball’s 1940 season finished 3-7, thanks in large part to injuries piled on top of a host of graduates from the 1939 team, including future NFLers Tommy Mont and Jim Gaffney.
The Campers in 1941 capped off their first unblemished season in school history with a 19-0 romp over Fort Hill on Turkey Day for a 9-0 finish.
The West Siders were again victorious in 1942’s Turkey Day affair, a 17-6 win over the Sentinels to seal a second straight undefeated season at 8-0.
Part of Allegany’s success in ‘41 and ‘42 was due to Ball implementing the T-formation that was sweeping the nation thanks in large part to the Chicago Bears, coached by the legendary George Halas, and Clark Shaughnessy, who left Stanford after the 1941 season amid fears that the university was going to cut the football program due to the war.
Following his departure from Stanford, Shaughnessy signed a “lifetime contract” at Maryland. With the Terps, Shaughnessy installed a pass-oriented version of the T-formation, leading to Mont, Maryland’s starting quarterback, being named an honorable mention All-American and the No. 3 passer in the country.
Ball’s reign as Allegany’s football coach came to an abrupt end in February 1943 when he submitted his resignation due to an “ignored” salary increase request.
“I first conferred with Charles L. Kopp, superintendent of schools, on July 1, 1942, relative to an increase in my salary of $1,980 for serving as football coach, a member of the teaching staff and assistant principal,” Ball said in the Feb. 8, 1943, edition of The Cumberland News.
“Since that time on several occasions, I have talked to Superintendent Kopp and two members of the board in connection with my request, and in each instance, I was advised that the matter would be settled at the next meeting.
texts.2:
“A number of meetings of the board have been held since July of last year, and so far Superintendent Kopp and the board members have not even extended to me the courtesy of a reply containing their refusal or approval.”
Ball’s time with the Campers ended with a record of 54-13-1.
“It is with great regret that I leave Allegany,” Ball said in the same interview. “I’ve had many happy associations there and I would not be leaving except that I feel that I’ve been ignored in my efforts to secure an adjustment in salary.”
Ball’s resignation sparked mass outrage, especially among the Allegany student body.
Nearly 40% of the school’s 1,525 students participated in a walkout on Feb. 9, 1943. The students paraded past the Board of Education offices on Washington Street and then marched to Fort Hill High School, where the group of 607 picked up approximately 100 sympathetic Sentinels to join their cause.
Despite Ball’s insistence that the students not take action on his behalf, the group descended upon Baltimore Street with chants of “We Want Ball,” No Coach, No School” and even some chants against the school’s administration.
Ball’s resignation was accepted by the Board of Education on Feb. 12, 1943.
A move to College Park
On July 8, 1943, two days before the Allied forces launched Operation Husky — a massive amphibious and airborne invasion of the Italian island of Sicily — Ball was hired by the University of Maryland to assist in its physical fitness training program for approximately 1,100 Army trainees.
Clarence “Doc” Spears said that if Maryland was to have a football team in the fall, Ball would be on his staff. Spears took over as head coach of the Maryland football team when Shaughnessy left the Terps after just one year to lead the football program at Pitt.
The Terps did have football that fall, with just one player with collegiate varsity experience answering Spears’ call for help.
Of the nearly 400 male students at Maryland who showed interest in playing football that fall — the Army trainees were not eligible — Spears and his staff whittled it down to around 50.
texts.3:
Many of the players had no high school football experience, let alone game time at any collegiate level, so the first day of practice was spent doing the fundamentals: passing, kicking, snapping and tackling.
Spears, Ball and Co. finished 4-5 that year, with a 2-0 mark in Southeastern Conference play with wins over Wake Forest and VMI.
Back in Cumberland, Bowers took over as Allegany head coach for the second time, with this stint spanning three seasons.
After a 5-4 mark in 1943, Bowers and the Campers went 9-1 and 8-0-1 before Bob Pence took over in 1946.
Ball remained on the Maryland staff for the 1944 season, when the Terps finished 1-7-1 with a season-concluding 8-6 victory over VMI.
In August of 1945, following Spears’ resignation, Maryland president H.C. Byrd denied reports that Ball had been named head coach.
The school ultimately hired the legendary Bear Bryant, who went 6-2-1 in his lone season in College Park before leaving for Kentucky, in part due to his tumultuous relationship with Byrd.
Ball, however, continued his ascent up the football ladder in 1945.
Still a member of Bryant’s staff at Maryland, Ball was appointed as a part-time scout with the Washington Redskins in August 1945.
In the Dec. 27, 1945, edition of the Cumberland Evening Times, it was reported that the Redskins were pursuing a trade for Mont to join Gaffney, who was drafted by the Redskins in 1944.
The deal would send Frankie Filchock to the New York Giants for Mont and Paul Stenn, with Mont joining the Redskins upon his discharge from the military. Mont was serving in the Army and stationed in Germany.
A slightly altered trade went through a few weeks later, with the Redskins shipping Filchock to New York in exchange for Stenn and a player to be named later.
Following his military service, Mont — and Shaughnessy — returned to Maryland in 1946. Mont was joined by two Cumberlanders on the team in Fort Hill’s Fred Davis and LaSalle’s Norman Geatz.
texts.4:
In May 1947, Mont, the player to be named later in the trade a year prior with the Giants, signed a contract with the Redskins.
In 1946, Ball stepped down from his post as an assistant at Maryland to join the Redskins in a full-time capacity as scout.
Head man for the Redskins
The departure from Maryland lasted only months, as it was announced in September that Ball was rejoining the Maryland coaching staff in an undisclosed, but presumably minor, role.
Ball remained with the Redskins and, in 1949, was appointed as the team’s line coach under new head coach John Whelchel.
There were widespread reports in Washington of coaching departures, including Ball, following a 49-14 thrashing at the hands of the Eagles on Oct. 23, 1949.
Two weeks later, Whelchel was fired after a 3-3-1 start to the year.
Ball, 39 years old at the time, was named head coach — the Redskins went 1-4 the rest of the way, notching a 30-0 win over the Packers in the second-to-last game of the season.
Although Ball wasn’t officially given an interim tag, Washington owner George Preston Marshall reiterated in January 1950 that Ball would remain as head coach for the upcoming season.
After an undefeated preseason and 38-14 win over the Baltimore Colts in the season opener, the Redskins lost seven straight and finished 3-9.
Ball and the Redskins got off to an 0-3 start to the 1951 campaign, and Ball was fired as a result on Oct. 18.
The decision led to a bizarre situation as it was widely reported that Bears assistant Hunk Anderson would be the new head coach. Anderson was prevented from starting his new post due to contract issues with Chicago’s George Halas and, after Marshall refused to provide the Bears with compensation, Ball’s assistant Dick Todd was named interim head coach.
Ball returned to his old post as chief scout before resigning on Dec. 17, 1954, after briefly returning to the Washington sidelines as an assistant.
Weeks after his resignation, Ball was hired as an assistant with the Pittsburgh Steelers.
texts.5:
Ball’s tenure in the Steel City lasted one season, taking a job as a line coach and scout with the Baltimore Colts on Feb. 2, 1956.
Ball stayed with the Colts for seven years, capturing back-to-back NFL titles in 1958 and 1959.
Ball was dismissed after the 1962 season when Colts head coach Weeb Ewbank was replaced by Don Shula.
Ball left the NFL for the AFL’s Buffalo Bills, which was a short-lived stint, as he returned to the NFL a year later when former Redskins coach Joe Kuharich was hired by the Philadelphia Eagles.
Kuharich and his staff were fired after a 2-12 finish in 1968, but Ball stayed in Philadelphia as the team’s director of player personnel.
In 1977, Ball announced his retirement after a career that spanned 34 years in the NFL. He stayed with the Eagles in an advisory role until 1986.
“Herman is one of the distinguished gentlemen in the NFL,” said then-Eagles coach Dick Vermeil. “We all have a great deal of admiration and respect for him and feel very fortunate that he has agreed to remain close to the organization in an advisory capacity.”
In 1985, Ball was inducted into the Allegany Hall of Fame.
Fourteen years later, on Jan. 12, 1999, Ball died at the age of 88.
Cavanaugh’s influence on city sports
While Ball’s legacy mostly spanned the professional ranks, Cavanaugh left a lasting impact on Cumberland and Allegany County.
A native New Englander, Cavanaugh played football, basketball, baseball and ice hockey at Crosby High School in Waterbury, Connecticut.
Cumberland wasn’t on his radar until his graduation from Washington College on Maryland’s Eastern Shore when Cavanaugh heard that Penn Avenue was seeking someone to coach “all types of sports.”
From 1928, when he was hired, until 1935, when Penn Avenue closed its high school program, Cavanaugh coached six sports: basketball, soccer, baseball, track, swimming and football. He even taught tumbling at one time.
texts.6:
Cavanaugh was the referee in the first Thanksgiving Day football game played between city rivals when Allegany obliterated LaSalle, 59-0, at Mid-City Park in 1928.
When Penn Avenue decided to start its football program in the fall of 1932, Cavanaugh inherited the football job as a one-man coaching staff.
In 1935, Cavanaugh’s Maroons won the City championship, beating LaSalle, 24-0, and Allegany, 20-6, and finished 7-1-1.
Cavanaugh’s Penn Avenue squads went 11-12-8 in four seasons.
Losses bookended Cavanaugh’s first and only season as Fort Hill football head coach — the Sentinels fell to Windber, Pennsylvania, 56-6, in the season opener before losing to Allegany in the first Turkey Day game between the Campers and Sentinels.
Fort Hill finished its inaugural season 6-2 and Johnny Long became head coach in 1937, lightening Cavanaugh’s load and allowing him to coach basketball and baseball.
Cavanaugh’s legacy on the hardwood spanned 30 years between Fort Hill and Penn Avenue between 1929 and 1958, compiling a record of 525-216 with seven state championships.
Four of Cavanaugh’s state championships came during the pre-Maryland Public Secondary Schools Athletic Association era, when Cumberland schools won 12 of the 13 state championships between 1927 and 1939.
Bowers, who won 11 state titles with a 567-164 record at Allegany, won the state crown in 1927, five in a row from 1930 to 1934 and two straight in 1936 and 1937.
Catonsville won the 1928 championship.
Cavanaugh won state crowns at Penn Avenue in 1929 and 1935, with back-to-back championships at Fort Hill in 1938 and 1939.
No state tournaments were played 1940-1946 due to the war, and the MPSSAA began hosting state tourneys in 1947.

Mar. 29—CUMBERLAND — For just the second time in the 50-year history of the award, a lineman has won area Player of the Year.
Carter Hess, standing at 6-foot-2, 295 pounds, kept opposing head coaches up at night over the past three seasons, and he'll likely keep them up in college too, playing for Division 1 Fordham University next fall.
Advertisement
It was unsurprising then, that Hess was the runaway pick for the area's top player by those same coaches.
The right tackle and interior defensive line standout will receive the award at the 75th Dick Sterne Memorial Dapper Dan Sports Banquet on Sunday, April 28, at 4 p.m. in the Ali Ghan Shrine Club Ballroom.
"I would venture to say he's one of the best players to ever play at Fort Hill," his head coach Zack Alkire said. "The more that we asked Carter to do, the better he'd get at it."
Hess received all but two Player of the Year votes, with the other two going to Will Patterson, who shared Offensive Player of the Year honors with Sentinel back Jabril Daniels on Thursday.
Advertisement
The Fort Hill lineman has won an award in every full varsity football season he's played. Hess was area Defensive Player of the Year last year and Lineman of the Year in 2021.
The rest of the state finally realized Hess' dominance this year, something this area's head coaches were already painfully aware of.
He was the recipient of Class 1A state Player of the Year by the Maryland Football Foundation and MPSSAA Defensive Player of the Year, regardless of class, by Baltimore Sports and Life.
It was fitting, then, that Hess ended a 24-year drought since the last time a lineman was this area's Player of the Year, achieving the feat only Moorefield's Justin Williams, who went on to play at West Virginia University, did in 1999.
Advertisement
At the time, Williams was the first lineman in West Virginia scholastic football history to start on four state championship-winning teams.
Hess never got that chance because his freshman year was shorted by the COVID-19 pandemic, but he did star on three Maryland Class 1A champions, and Fort Hill was 38-1 over that span.
texts.1:
While Hess' strength is well-documented, Alkire highlighted his technique and preparation as things that set the senior apart.
"People think about how strong he is, but he has great feet, hands and quickness," Alkire said. "He sees the field well, and that's because of his intelligence. He's always in the right spot because he studies.
Advertisement
"You can see how much film everybody watches, and every day he's the leader, watching 3-4 hours more than the next kid."
Hess finished his final campaign in red and white as the area's leading tackler for a second straight year, racking up 145 of them (74 solos) to go along with an area-best 13 sacks, 23 tackles for loss and four forced fumbles.
For the under-recruited Hess, who would've played Power 5 football if he was three inches taller, it all began in the weight room.
"He's a very self-motivated player. He worked his tail off," said Alkire. "He had to work harder than everybody else because all eyes were on him. Even though he was self-motivated, he expected the same out of everybody else.
Advertisement
"Most of the guys aren't going to work as hard as him, but he expected his teammates to approach that level. He never took plays off, even in practice. When they weren't giving him their best, he'd let them know and when Carter Hess spoke, people listened."
It was difficult for Hess to go 100% in practice all year out of fear that he might injure the players going against him.
Fort Hill had no junior linemen in its program in 2023, prompting Fort Hill to call up a collection of sophomores to groom them for the starting role next year.
"Carter's biggest obstacle is he had put himself in a position where unless we would take one of our starters out, it was difficult for him as the season moved forward to work as hard in practice," Alkire said.
Advertisement
"He was going against much younger, smaller kids in practice. As the season progressed, he found that middle ground again where he could push himself without taking it too far. ... By doing that, he made the whole team better."
texts.2:
Hess' work ethic was instilled by his father, Sam Hess, who still holds the state record for rushing yards in a game after he ran for 446 yards as Hancock's star running back against St. James in 1998.
Carter is now the third person in his immediate family to earn a collegiate sports scholarship. His father went on to play at Shepherd University, and his sister, Chloe Hess, is in her sophomore year as the ace of Lehigh's softball team — she was second-team All-Patriot League as a freshman.
Carter Hess won state championships at Fort Hill across three sports.
Advertisement
Hess became Fort Hill's first individual wrestling state champion since Dave Phillips took home the 189-pound state title in 1990 when he won the 285-pound Class 2A/1A championship this winter to complete an unbeaten 33-0 season.
Hess is also the two-time defending Maryland Class 1A discus state champion, setting a state record last spring with a 168-foot heave.
Coaches in the Western Maryland Athletic Conference can now breathe a sigh of relief because Hess is the Patriot League's problem.
And there's little doubt in Alkire's mind that his prized lineman will be a problem at the next level.
Advertisement
"I think him going to Fordham, he'll see the field sooner rather than later," Alkire said. "It's a good situation. He's going to be the hardest worker in the room. I believe he's going to make his presence felt Day 1 and earn some playing time as a freshman. He's going to be a very good player in that league."
Alex Rychwalski is a sports reporter at the Cumberland Times-News. Follow him on Twitter @arychwal.

Prior to the Revolutionary War, the Cherokee called the land Esseneca. William Bartram visited this Lower Town twice, writing that it “is a respectable settlement, situated on the East Bank of the Keowee river.”
Before Fort Hill, the antebellum plantation of John C. Calhoun, South Carolina’s pre-eminent 19th century statesman, there was four-room Clergy Hall. Originally built in 1803, Clergy Hall served as the manse or parsonage for nearby Hopewell-Keowee Church, now known as Old Stone Presbyterian Church. Next, Floride Bonneau Colhoun, John C. Calhoun’s mother-in-law, purchased the 600 acre property; U.S. Vice President Calhoun’s family called the expanded structure Fort Hill, starting in 1830, after Revolutionary War Fort Rutledge.
In total, ten rooms were added to the structure and additional acreage was purchased by John C. Calhoun; however, he was not the owner until 1836, after the death of his mother-in-law.When John C. died in 1850, his wife Floride became the sole owner of the Fort Hill home and 1,341 acres of land. When she passed in 1866, portions of the property then went to their daughter and sole surviving child, Anna Maria Calhoun, who had married Thomas Green Clemson in 1838. The Clemsons’ daughter, Floride Elizabeth, also inherited a portion. Tragically, Anna Calhoun Clemson did not take ownership of land until her two surviving children had already passed.
Anna Maria Calhoun Clemson willed her three-fourths share of Fort Hill to her husband, Thomas Clemson, with the caveat that he must die with a will. At Anna’s death in 1875, Thomas worked with two attorneys, James Rion and Richard Wright Simpson, to create his bequest that became Clemson University. If he had not, the granddaughter Floride Isabella Lee would have inherited the entire property in accordance with Anna Clemson’s will.

Through a succession of Calhoun-Clemson women, Fort Hill would come into Thomas Green Clemson’s possession. In 1888, Clemson bequeathed three-fourths of the Fort Hill plantation and $80,000 to the state of South Carolina for the establishment of a public scientific and agricultural college. He willed that Fort Hill “shall always be open for the inspection of visitors.”
Today, Fort Hill is just as Thomas Clemson envisioned — preserved, restored and open to the public for tours.
The enslaved African-Americans, whose story of resistance and resilience left little written records, built and operated from 1825 through 1865., Prior to Anna Clemson inheriting Fort Hill on January 21, 1872, Thomas Green Clemson began signing employment contracts in 1868 with former enslaved persons from Fort Hill and neighboring plantations.
**Freedman's Contracts**
Signed by Thomas Green Clemson
Life at Fort Hill, and all of its financial growth, was only possible because of the physical labor and sheer determination of the enslaved African Americans who toiled on the 450 acre cultivated land, producing maintaining the household, and performing construction of the plantation.
Since the enslaved who occupied Fort Hill left no written record, their perspective has been made virtually voiceless in history. In many cases, names and family connections are not known.
**African Americans at Fort Hill – Primary Documents**
1854 and 1865
Little is known about the families who were enslaved at Fort Hill by its three plantation era owners, John C. Calhoun, Floride Colhoun Calhoun, and Andrew Pickens Calhoun. There are records of a few family units, including: Sawney, his wife Tiller, and at least two of their children, Sawney Jr. and Issey; Daphne, her husband Bill Lawrence, and their children Susan Clemson Richardson and Benjamin; Sharper, his wife Caroline, and his daughter Tiller; and Nelly and her son Andy.
Read more about African Americans at Fort Hill.
