October 30, 2026 by
CUMBERLAND — A tradition that has lasted 90 years and counting isn’t the only thing Cumberland got from the inaugural meeting between Allegany and Fort Hill on Thanksgiving Day in 1936.
The game, which Allegany won, 19-17, featured two head coaches — Herman Ball and John J. “Bobby” Cavanaugh — who had remarkable legacies beyond the Cumberland gridiron.
On one side at Community Park was Herman Ball, who was putting the finishing touches on a 9-0-1 season in his inaugural campaign as Allegany’s head ball coach.
Ball, an Elkins, West Virginia, native, attended Davis & Elkins College and played at guard on the 1933 team that led all of college football in points scored with 345. Ball played under Cam Henderson, who was featured in Ripley’s Believe It or Not in 1933 for coaching all sports at Davis & Elkins without assistants, trainers or scouts.
Following his time at Davis & Elkins, Ball was hired as head coach at Ridgeley in 1935, finishing 3-3-1 before crossing the Potomac to take the same post at Allegany.
Ball not only won the first Turkey Day game between Allegany and Fort Hill, but he also was the first of five Allegany head coaches to win their first Turkey Day/Homecoming game against Fort Hill.
Bill Bowers, in his second stint as Allegany head coach, won in 1943, 14-7. George Stimmel won The Snow Game in 1971, 18-14. Jack Gilmore shut out the Sentinels in 1985, 24-0. Tim Foley, serving as interim head coach while Tom Preaskorn was in Iraq as a major in the West Virginia Army National Guard, won the 2007 matchup, 33-14.
Ball coached the Campers for seven seasons and was 6-1 against the Sentinels, with the lone loss a 20-0 defeat in 1940.

After his opening campaign, Ball’s next three Allegany squads had three straight 8-2 seasons — outside of a 20-0 loss to Waynesburg (Pennsylvania) in 1937, the Campers lost by no more than seven points during those three seasons.
Ball’s 1940 season finished 3-7, thanks in large part to injuries piled on top of a host of graduates from the 1939 team, including future NFLers Tommy Mont and Jim Gaffney.
The Campers in 1941 capped off their first unblemished season in school history with a 19-0 romp over Fort Hill on Turkey Day for a 9-0 finish.
The West Siders were again victorious in 1942’s Turkey Day affair, a 17-6 win over the Sentinels to seal a second straight undefeated season at 8-0.
Part of Allegany’s success in ‘41 and ‘42 was due to Ball implementing the T-formation that was sweeping the nation thanks in large part to the Chicago Bears, coached by the legendary George Halas, and Clark Shaughnessy, who left Stanford after the 1941 season amid fears that the university was going to cut the football program due to the war.
Following his departure from Stanford, Shaughnessy signed a “lifetime contract” at Maryland. With the Terps, Shaughnessy installed a pass-oriented version of the T-formation, leading to Mont, Maryland’s starting quarterback, being named an honorable mention All-American and the No. 3 passer in the country.
Ball’s reign as Allegany’s football coach came to an abrupt end in February 1943 when he submitted his resignation due to an “ignored” salary increase request.
“I first conferred with Charles L. Kopp, superintendent of schools, on July 1, 1942, relative to an increase in my salary of $1,980 for serving as football coach, a member of the teaching staff and assistant principal,” Ball said in the Feb. 8, 1943, edition of The Cumberland News.
“Since that time on several occasions, I have talked to Superintendent Kopp and two members of the board in connection with my request, and in each instance, I was advised that the matter would be settled at the next meeting.

“A number of meetings of the board have been held since July of last year, and so far Superintendent Kopp and the board members have not even extended to me the courtesy of a reply containing their refusal or approval.”
Ball’s time with the Campers ended with a record of 54-13-1.
“It is with great regret that I leave Allegany,” Ball said in the same interview. “I’ve had many happy associations there and I would not be leaving except that I feel that I’ve been ignored in my efforts to secure an adjustment in salary.”
Ball’s resignation sparked mass outrage, especially among the Allegany student body.
Nearly 40% of the school’s 1,525 students participated in a walkout on Feb. 9, 1943. The students paraded past the Board of Education offices on Washington Street and then marched to Fort Hill High School, where the group of 607 picked up approximately 100 sympathetic Sentinels to join their cause.
Despite Ball’s insistence that the students not take action on his behalf, the group descended upon Baltimore Street with chants of “We Want Ball,” No Coach, No School” and even some chants against the school’s administration.
Ball’s resignation was accepted by the Board of Education on Feb. 12, 1943.
A move to College Park
On July 8, 1943, two days before the Allied forces launched Operation Husky — a massive amphibious and airborne invasion of the Italian island of Sicily — Ball was hired by the University of Maryland to assist in its physical fitness training program for approximately 1,100 Army trainees.
Clarence “Doc” Spears said that if Maryland was to have a football team in the fall, Ball would be on his staff. Spears took over as head coach of the Maryland football team when Shaughnessy left the Terps after just one year to lead the football program at Pitt.
The Terps did have football that fall, with just one player with collegiate varsity experience answering Spears’ call for help.
Of the nearly 400 male students at Maryland who showed interest in playing football that fall — the Army trainees were not eligible — Spears and his staff whittled it down to around 50.

Many of the players had no high school football experience, let alone game time at any collegiate level, so the first day of practice was spent doing the fundamentals: passing, kicking, snapping and tackling.
Spears, Ball and Co. finished 4-5 that year, with a 2-0 mark in Southeastern Conference play with wins over Wake Forest and VMI.
Back in Cumberland, Bowers took over as Allegany head coach for the second time, with this stint spanning three seasons.
After a 5-4 mark in 1943, Bowers and the Campers went 9-1 and 8-0-1 before Bob Pence took over in 1946.
Ball remained on the Maryland staff for the 1944 season, when the Terps finished 1-7-1 with a season-concluding 8-6 victory over VMI.
In August of 1945, following Spears’ resignation, Maryland president H.C. Byrd denied reports that Ball had been named head coach.
The school ultimately hired the legendary Bear Bryant, who went 6-2-1 in his lone season in College Park before leaving for Kentucky, in part due to his tumultuous relationship with Byrd.
Ball, however, continued his ascent up the football ladder in 1945.
Still a member of Bryant’s staff at Maryland, Ball was appointed as a part-time scout with the Washington Redskins in August 1945.
In the Dec. 27, 1945, edition of the Cumberland Evening Times, it was reported that the Redskins were pursuing a trade for Mont to join Gaffney, who was drafted by the Redskins in 1944.
The deal would send Frankie Filchock to the New York Giants for Mont and Paul Stenn, with Mont joining the Redskins upon his discharge from the military. Mont was serving in the Army and stationed in Germany.
A slightly altered trade went through a few weeks later, with the Redskins shipping Filchock to New York in exchange for Stenn and a player to be named later.
Following his military service, Mont — and Shaughnessy — returned to Maryland in 1946. Mont was joined by two Cumberlanders on the team in Fort Hill’s Fred Davis and LaSalle’s Norman Geatz.

In May 1947, Mont, the player to be named later in the trade a year prior with the Giants, signed a contract with the Redskins.
In 1946, Ball stepped down from his post as an assistant at Maryland to join the Redskins in a full-time capacity as scout.
Head man for the Redskins
The departure from Maryland lasted only months, as it was announced in September that Ball was rejoining the Maryland coaching staff in an undisclosed, but presumably minor, role.
Ball remained with the Redskins and, in 1949, was appointed as the team’s line coach under new head coach John Whelchel.
There were widespread reports in Washington of coaching departures, including Ball, following a 49-14 thrashing at the hands of the Eagles on Oct. 23, 1949.
Two weeks later, Whelchel was fired after a 3-3-1 start to the year.
Ball, 39 years old at the time, was named head coach — the Redskins went 1-4 the rest of the way, notching a 30-0 win over the Packers in the second-to-last game of the season.
Although Ball wasn’t officially given an interim tag, Washington owner George Preston Marshall reiterated in January 1950 that Ball would remain as head coach for the upcoming season.
After an undefeated preseason and 38-14 win over the Baltimore Colts in the season opener, the Redskins lost seven straight and finished 3-9.
Ball and the Redskins got off to an 0-3 start to the 1951 campaign, and Ball was fired as a result on Oct. 18.
The decision led to a bizarre situation as it was widely reported that Bears assistant Hunk Anderson would be the new head coach. Anderson was prevented from starting his new post due to contract issues with Chicago’s George Halas and, after Marshall refused to provide the Bears with compensation, Ball’s assistant Dick Todd was named interim head coach.
Ball returned to his old post as chief scout before resigning on Dec. 17, 1954, after briefly returning to the Washington sidelines as an assistant.
Weeks after his resignation, Ball was hired as an assistant with the Pittsburgh Steelers.

Ball’s tenure in the Steel City lasted one season, taking a job as a line coach and scout with the Baltimore Colts on Feb. 2, 1956.
Ball stayed with the Colts for seven years, capturing back-to-back NFL titles in 1958 and 1959.
Ball was dismissed after the 1962 season when Colts head coach Weeb Ewbank was replaced by Don Shula.
Ball left the NFL for the AFL’s Buffalo Bills, which was a short-lived stint, as he returned to the NFL a year later when former Redskins coach Joe Kuharich was hired by the Philadelphia Eagles.
Kuharich and his staff were fired after a 2-12 finish in 1968, but Ball stayed in Philadelphia as the team’s director of player personnel.
In 1977, Ball announced his retirement after a career that spanned 34 years in the NFL. He stayed with the Eagles in an advisory role until 1986.
“Herman is one of the distinguished gentlemen in the NFL,” said then-Eagles coach Dick Vermeil. “We all have a great deal of admiration and respect for him and feel very fortunate that he has agreed to remain close to the organization in an advisory capacity.”
In 1985, Ball was inducted into the Allegany Hall of Fame.
Fourteen years later, on Jan. 12, 1999, Ball died at the age of 88.
Cavanaugh’s influence on city sports
While Ball’s legacy mostly spanned the professional ranks, Cavanaugh left a lasting impact on Cumberland and Allegany County.
A native New Englander, Cavanaugh played football, basketball, baseball and ice hockey at Crosby High School in Waterbury, Connecticut.
Cumberland wasn’t on his radar until his graduation from Washington College on Maryland’s Eastern Shore when Cavanaugh heard that Penn Avenue was seeking someone to coach “all types of sports.”
From 1928, when he was hired, until 1935, when Penn Avenue closed its high school program, Cavanaugh coached six sports: basketball, soccer, baseball, track, swimming and football. He even taught tumbling at one time.

Cavanaugh was the referee in the first Thanksgiving Day football game played between city rivals when Allegany obliterated LaSalle, 59-0, at Mid-City Park in 1928.
When Penn Avenue decided to start its football program in the fall of 1932, Cavanaugh inherited the football job as a one-man coaching staff.
In 1935, Cavanaugh’s Maroons won the City championship, beating LaSalle, 24-0, and Allegany, 20-6, and finished 7-1-1.
Cavanaugh’s Penn Avenue squads went 11-12-8 in four seasons.
Losses bookended Cavanaugh’s first and only season as Fort Hill football head coach — the Sentinels fell to Windber, Pennsylvania, 56-6, in the season opener before losing to Allegany in the first Turkey Day game between the Campers and Sentinels.
Fort Hill finished its inaugural season 6-2 and Johnny Long became head coach in 1937, lightening Cavanaugh’s load and allowing him to coach basketball and baseball.
Cavanaugh’s legacy on the hardwood spanned 30 years between Fort Hill and Penn Avenue between 1929 and 1958, compiling a record of 525-216 with seven state championships.
Four of Cavanaugh’s state championships came during the pre-Maryland Public Secondary Schools Athletic Association era, when Cumberland schools won 12 of the 13 state championships between 1927 and 1939.
Bowers, who won 11 state titles with a 567-164 record at Allegany, won the state crown in 1927, five in a row from 1930 to 1934 and two straight in 1936 and 1937.
Catonsville won the 1928 championship.
Cavanaugh won state crowns at Penn Avenue in 1929 and 1935, with back-to-back championships at Fort Hill in 1938 and 1939.
No state tournaments were played 1940-1946 due to the war, and the MPSSAA began hosting state tourneys in 1947.

Title: Fort Hill lineman Carter Hess wins Player of the Year
Chunks: 0,1,2
Mar. 29—CUMBERLAND — For just the second time in the 50-year history of the award, a lineman has won area Player of the Year.
Carter Hess, standing at 6-foot-2, 295 pounds, kept opposing head coaches up at night over the past three seasons, and he'll likely keep them up in college too, playing for Division 1 Fordham University next fall.
Advertisement
It was unsurprising then, that Hess was the runaway pick for the area's top player by those same coaches.
The right tackle and interior defensive line standout will receive the award at the 75th Dick Sterne Memorial Dapper Dan Sports Banquet on Sunday, April 28, at 4 p.m. in the Ali Ghan Shrine Club Ballroom.
"I would venture to say he's one of the best players to ever play at Fort Hill," his head coach Zack Alkire said. "The more that we asked Carter to do, the better he'd get at it."
Hess received all but two Player of the Year votes, with the other two going to Will Patterson, who shared Offensive Player of the Year honors with Sentinel back Jabril Daniels on Thursday.
Advertisement
The Fort Hill lineman has won an award in every full varsity football season he's played. Hess was area Defensive Player of the Year last year and Lineman of the Year in 2021.
The rest of the state finally realized Hess' dominance this year, something this area's head coaches were already painfully aware of.
He was the recipient of Class 1A state Player of the Year by the Maryland Football Foundation and MPSSAA Defensive Player of the Year, regardless of class, by Baltimore Sports and Life.
It was fitting, then, that Hess ended a 24-year drought since the last time a lineman was this area's Player of the Year, achieving the feat only Moorefield's Justin Williams, who went on to play at West Virginia University, did in 1999.
Advertisement
At the time, Williams was the first lineman in West Virginia scholastic football history to start on four state championship-winning teams.
Hess never got that chance because his freshman year was shorted by the COVID-19 pandemic, but he did star on three Maryland Class 1A champions, and Fort Hill was 38-1 over that span.

While Hess' strength is well-documented, Alkire highlighted his technique and preparation as things that set the senior apart.
"People think about how strong he is, but he has great feet, hands and quickness," Alkire said. "He sees the field well, and that's because of his intelligence. He's always in the right spot because he studies.
Advertisement
"You can see how much film everybody watches, and every day he's the leader, watching 3-4 hours more than the next kid."
Hess finished his final campaign in red and white as the area's leading tackler for a second straight year, racking up 145 of them (74 solos) to go along with an area-best 13 sacks, 23 tackles for loss and four forced fumbles.
For the under-recruited Hess, who would've played Power 5 football if he was three inches taller, it all began in the weight room.
"He's a very self-motivated player. He worked his tail off," said Alkire. "He had to work harder than everybody else because all eyes were on him. Even though he was self-motivated, he expected the same out of everybody else.
Advertisement
"Most of the guys aren't going to work as hard as him, but he expected his teammates to approach that level. He never took plays off, even in practice. When they weren't giving him their best, he'd let them know and when Carter Hess spoke, people listened."
It was difficult for Hess to go 100% in practice all year out of fear that he might injure the players going against him.
Fort Hill had no junior linemen in its program in 2023, prompting Fort Hill to call up a collection of sophomores to groom them for the starting role next year.
"Carter's biggest obstacle is he had put himself in a position where unless we would take one of our starters out, it was difficult for him as the season moved forward to work as hard in practice," Alkire said.
Advertisement
"He was going against much younger, smaller kids in practice. As the season progressed, he found that middle ground again where he could push himself without taking it too far. ... By doing that, he made the whole team better."

Hess' work ethic was instilled by his father, Sam Hess, who still holds the state record for rushing yards in a game after he ran for 446 yards as Hancock's star running back against St. James in 1998.
Carter is now the third person in his immediate family to earn a collegiate sports scholarship. His father went on to play at Shepherd University, and his sister, Chloe Hess, is in her sophomore year as the ace of Lehigh's softball team — she was second-team All-Patriot League as a freshman.
Carter Hess won state championships at Fort Hill across three sports.
Advertisement
Hess became Fort Hill's first individual wrestling state champion since Dave Phillips took home the 189-pound state title in 1990 when he won the 285-pound Class 2A/1A championship this winter to complete an unbeaten 33-0 season.
Hess is also the two-time defending Maryland Class 1A discus state champion, setting a state record last spring with a 168-foot heave.
Coaches in the Western Maryland Athletic Conference can now breathe a sigh of relief because Hess is the Patriot League's problem.
And there's little doubt in Alkire's mind that his prized lineman will be a problem at the next level.
Advertisement
"I think him going to Fordham, he'll see the field sooner rather than later," Alkire said. "It's a good situation. He's going to be the hardest worker in the room. I believe he's going to make his presence felt Day 1 and earn some playing time as a freshman. He's going to be a very good player in that league."
Alex Rychwalski is a sports reporter at the Cumberland Times-News. Follow him on Twitter @arychwal.

The **Clemson Tigers football** program are the American football team at Clemson University. The Tigers compete in the NCAA Division IFootball Bowl Subdivision (FBS) of the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) of the Atlantic Coast Conference (ACC).

Formed in 1896, the program has an all-time record of 804–473–44,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-2) with a bowl record of 27–23. Clemson was a College Football Playoff finalist in 2015, 2016, 2018, and 2019, defeating Alabama in both 2016 and 2018 to secure the national title. Clemson has had six undefeated seasons (including the first-ever 15–0 team), boasted six consecutive playoff appearances from 2015 to 2021, and retains 27 conference championships, including 8 since 2011. Its alumni include over 100 All-Americans, 17 Academic All-Americans and over 250 players in the National Football League.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-4) Clemson has had eight members inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame: players Banks McFadden, Terry Kinard, Jeff Davis, and C. J. Spiller along with coaches John Heisman, Jess Neely, Frank Howard, and Danny Ford.

Clemson is one of the founding members of the ACC and holds 22 ACC titles, the most of any member. Its 28 total conference titles, including six consecutive ACC titles from 2015 to 2020, are the most of any ACC school. Clemson's most recent ACC title came in 2024, against SMU. Clemson's streak of eleven consecutive 10-win seasons from 2011-2022 ranked second in active streaks behind the Alabama Crimson Tide, coming to an end after Clemson's 2023 season where they finished with a 9–4 record.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-6) Among its eight undefeated regular seasons, Clemson has been crowned national champion 3 times. Clemson was named poll-era national champion and finished with its third perfect season with a win over Nebraska in the 1982 Orange Bowl. Clemson was the National Championship Finalist Runner-up with a 14–1 record in 2015 before winning the National Title over No. 1 Alabama in college football's first National Championship rematch in 2016, and again in 2018. However, Clemson then lost the next year to the undefeated LSU Tigers in the 2020 College Football Playoff National Championship 25-42. The Tigers have 46 bowl appearances, 20 of which are among the [New Year's Six](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Year's_Six "New Year's Six") Bowls, including nine during the "Big Four" era. Clemson has 34 finishes in the final top 25 in the modern era and it finished in either the Associated Press final poll or the coaches' final poll a combined 59 times since 1939.
The Tigers play their home games in Memorial Stadium on the university's Clemson, South Carolina campus. The stadium's nickname, "Death Valley" was coined in 1948 by Presbyterian College head coach Lonnie McMillan after his teams were routinely defeated there. Memorial Stadium is among the largest stadiums in college football.
Walter Riggs, the "father of Clemson football"

Walter Riggs, often regarded as the "father of Clemson football," brought the sport to Clemson from the Agricultural and Mechanical College of Alabama (now Auburn University). The team's first game, played on Halloween 1896, resulted in a 2–1 record for the inaugural season. Riggs influenced the choice of the team mascot and colors. The Tigers’ early success included their first undefeated season in 1900 under coach John W. Heisman, who led the team to a 19–3–2 record. Heisman’s coaching set a precedent for excellence and innovation.
During the mid-20th century, the program experienced substantial growth under Frank Howard, who coached from 1940 to 1969. Howard's tenure saw Clemson win two Southern Conference championships and six ACC championships. Known for his colorful personality and imaginative storytelling, Howard integrated various offensive formations. His legacy includes the tradition of rubbing "Howard's Rock" before home games and the naming of the playing field at Memorial Stadium as "Frank Howard Field" in 1974.
The late 20th century and early 21st century saw the football program navigate through challenges and successes under multiple head coaches. Danny Ford led the Tigers to their first national championship in 1981, achieving an undefeated season. Ford's era was marked by NCAA sanctions due to recruiting violations, which impacted the program's reputation and success. Ken Hatfield, Ford’s successor, focused on cleaning up the program's image but faced criticism from fans, leading to his resignation. Subsequent coaches, including Tommy West, struggled to achieve consistent success until the hiring of Tommy Bowden in 1999, who maintained bowl eligibility every season, but failed to secure an ACC championship.
Coach Dabo Swinney

The modern era is defined by the leadership of Dabo Swinney, who became head coach in 2008. Swinney revitalized the program, leading the Tigers to multiple ACC championships and two national titles in 2016 and 2018. His tenure has been characterized by significant achievements, including the establishment of Clemson as a perennial contender in the College Football Playoff. Swinney’s ability to recruit and develop talent, combined with strategic hires like offensive coordinator Chad Morris and defensive coordinator Brent Venables, has sustained Clemson’s success. Notably, under Swinney, Clemson became the first team since 1897 to finish a season 15–0. In 2022, Clemson defeated Syracuse 27–21, extending the Tigers' home winning streak to 38, a new ACC record.

Members of the 2010 Clemson Tigers baseball team at Russ Chandler Stadium
As of 2018, the Tiger baseball team has posted a combined 32 ACC regular season and tournament championships (the most in the conference), 43 NCAA Tournament appearances, 17 NCAA Regional Titles, four NCAA Super Regional titles, and 12 College World Series appearances. Much of the baseball program's success occurred under Bill Wilhelm during his 35 seasons as Clemson's head coach. Erik Bakich is the Tigers' current head coach, having replaced Monte Lee after the conclusion of the 2022 season.

The Clemson men's basketball team has qualified for the [NCAA Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_men's_basketball_tournament "NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament") 13 times, and reached the Sweet 16 four times and the Elite Eight once. They are currently coached by Brad Brownell since 2010.
The Clemson women's basketball team began in 1975, and saw its biggest success in the late 1980s and 1990s. The Tigers reached the NCAA Elite Eight in 1991, and the Sweet Sixteen three times (1989, 1990, 1999). Women's basketball won two [ACC Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACC_women's_basketball_tournament "ACC women's basketball tournament") championships in 1996 and 1999, and the regular season title in 1981. The team is currently coached by Amanda Butler.
The Tigers take the field by running down the hill in Memorial Stadium's east end zone, 2006.
Clemson has three national championships in football, the most recent coming in 2018 with a victory over Alabama 44–16 in the 2019 College Football Playoff National Championship. Clemson has appeared in the last six playoffs and won two national championships during those visits. The Tigers also possess the most Atlantic Coast Conference championships with 20, including winning the last six.
It has also won greater than 60% of its games, placing it in the top 25 on the all-time winning percentage list. Clemson also won two Southern Conference titles before joining the ACC. The 1981 squad, led by Head Coach Danny Ford, became the first athletic team in school history to win a national championship. Clemson defeated Nebraska 22–15 in the Orange Bowl in Miami, Florida, to win the 1981 NCAA Football National Championship. Stars of the game included Homer Jordan (QB) and Perry Tuttle (WR). Clemson finished the year 12–0 and ranked #1 in the Associated Press and Coaches polls.

Some of the most notable coaching names in Clemson football history are John Heisman (who also coached at Akron, Auburn, Georgia Tech, Penn, Washington & Jefferson, and Rice; the Heisman Trophy is named after him), Jess Neely, Frank Howard (whom the playing field at Death Valley is named after), and Danny Ford. After Tommy Bowden resigned midseason on October 13, 2008, Dabo Swinney took over as interim head coach.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-ESPN-13) On December 1, 2008, Swinney was named head coach of the Clemson Tigers football team.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-14)
Before each home game, the team ends pre-game warm ups and proceeds to the locker room. With five minutes to go before game time, three buses leave the street behind the West Endzone carrying the Clemson football players. The buses pull to a stop at the gate in front of The Hill, and the Tigers gather at the top, where each player proceeds to rub "Howard's Rock", which is an imported rock from Death Valley, California that was presented to Frank Howard in 1967. While Tiger Rag is played and a cannon sounds, the Tigers run down the hill onto the field in front of over 83,000 screaming fans. This tradition has been dubbed "The most exciting 25 seconds in college football" by sportscaster Brent Musburger.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-15)

The Tiger men's golf team have a tradition of being among the best in the ACC and the nation, having won several ACC titles and regularly qualifying for the NCAA Tournament. In 2003, Clemson defeated Oklahoma State to win its first [National Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_Men's_Golf_Championships "NCAA Division I Men's Golf Championships") in golf and the 4th overall for the school.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-Golf_2003_NC-16) In addition to that victory, Clemson also won the ACC and NCAA East Regional titles that year, making the Tigers the first program in NCAA history to win its conference, regional, and national championship tournaments in the same year.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-Golf_2003_NC-16) Clemson has also won eight regional titles since the NCAA adopted the regional tournament format in 1989, with their most recent win coming in [2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_NCAA_Division_I_men's_golf_championship "2024 NCAA Division I men's golf championship").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-MG-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-18) Two Tigers have won individual NCAA Championships: Charles Warren in 1997 and Turk Pettit in 2021.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-MG-17)2009 U.S. Open champion Lucas Glover also played golf at Clemson.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-19)

### Discontinued varsity sports
Swimming & Diving  
The Tigers men's swimming & diving team was established in 1919, and won the Southern Conference championship in 1939, and the ACC team championship in 1986. The women's swimming & diving team began in 1975, and won 4 ACC championships (1987, 1988, 1989, 1997), and Mitzi Kremer won 4 NCAA championships. Both swimming teams and men's diving were discontinued after the 2012 season, and women's diving was discontinued after 2017.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlackman_et_al.2013209%E2%80%93217-35)
Wrestling  
Wrestling at Clemson University was discontinued in 1995, despite the success of the program, due to financial shortages from Tiger Athletics' funding from the university. The wrestling program began in 1975 winning the ACC title as a team under coach Eddie Griffin in 1991. The Tiger wrestling program produced eight All-Americans, two NCAA Champions, and a finish at the NCAA Championships as high as 7th in 1994.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-36)Noel Loban won Clemson's first national title in 1980, and went on to win a bronze medal in the 1984 Olympics. Sammie Henson is a former standout at Clemson, as one of the most accomplished Tiger wrestlers, with 1993 and 1994 NCAA Champion titles, who eventually earned a 2000 Olympics silver medal and became a World Champion in 1998 in freestyle wrestling.

As of 2018, the Tiger baseball team has posted a combined 32 ACC regular season and tournament championships (the most in the conference), 43 NCAA Tournament appearances, 17 NCAA Regional Titles, four NCAA Super Regional titles, and 12 College World Series appearances. Much of the baseball program's success occurred under Bill Wilhelm during his 35 seasons as Clemson's head coach. Erik Bakich is the Tigers' current head coach, having replaced Monte Lee after the conclusion of the 2022 season.
texts.4:
The Clemson men's basketball team has qualified for the [NCAA Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_men's_basketball_tournament "NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament") 13 times, and reached the Sweet 16 four times and the Elite Eight once. They are currently coached by Brad Brownell since 2010.
The Clemson women's basketball team began in 1975, and saw its biggest success in the late 1980s and 1990s. The Tigers reached the NCAA Elite Eight in 1991, and the Sweet Sixteen three times (1989, 1990, 1999). Women's basketball won two [ACC Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACC_women's_basketball_tournament "ACC women's basketball tournament") championships in 1996 and 1999, and the regular season title in 1981. The team is currently coached by Amanda Butler.
The Tigers take the field by running down the hill in Memorial Stadium's east end zone, 2006.
Clemson has three national championships in football, the most recent coming in 2018 with a victory over Alabama 44–16 in the 2019 College Football Playoff National Championship. Clemson has appeared in the last six playoffs and won two national championships during those visits. The Tigers also possess the most Atlantic Coast Conference championships with 20, including winning the last six.
It has also won greater than 60% of its games, placing it in the top 25 on the all-time winning percentage list. Clemson also won two Southern Conference titles before joining the ACC. The 1981 squad, led by Head Coach Danny Ford, became the first athletic team in school history to win a national championship. Clemson defeated Nebraska 22–15 in the Orange Bowl in Miami, Florida, to win the 1981 NCAA Football National Championship. Stars of the game included Homer Jordan (QB) and Perry Tuttle (WR). Clemson finished the year 12–0 and ranked #1 in the Associated Press and Coaches polls.
texts.5:
Some of the most notable coaching names in Clemson football history are John Heisman (who also coached at Akron, Auburn, Georgia Tech, Penn, Washington & Jefferson, and Rice; the Heisman Trophy is named after him), Jess Neely, Frank Howard (whom the playing field at Death Valley is named after), and Danny Ford. After Tommy Bowden resigned midseason on October 13, 2008, Dabo Swinney took over as interim head coach.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-ESPN-13) On December 1, 2008, Swinney was named head coach of the Clemson Tigers football team.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-14)
Before each home game, the team ends pre-game warm ups and proceeds to the locker room. With five minutes to go before game time, three buses leave the street behind the West Endzone carrying the Clemson football players. The buses pull to a stop at the gate in front of The Hill, and the Tigers gather at the top, where each player proceeds to rub "Howard's Rock", which is an imported rock from Death Valley, California that was presented to Frank Howard in 1967. While Tiger Rag is played and a cannon sounds, the Tigers run down the hill onto the field in front of over 83,000 screaming fans. This tradition has been dubbed "The most exciting 25 seconds in college football" by sportscaster Brent Musburger.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-15)
texts.6: The Tiger men's golf team have a tradition of being among the best in the ACC and the nation, having won several ACC titles and regularly qualifying for the NCAA Tournament. In 2003, Clemson defeated Oklahoma State to win its first [National Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_Men's_Golf_Championships "NCAA Division I Men's Golf Championships") in golf and the 4th overall for the school.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-Golf_2003_NC-16) In addition to that victory, Clemson also won the ACC and NCAA East Regional titles that year, making the Tigers the first program in NCAA history to win its conference, regional, and national championship tournaments in the same year.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-Golf_2003_NC-16) Clemson has also won eight regional titles since the NCAA adopted the regional tournament format in 1989, with their most recent win coming in [2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_NCAA_Division_I_men's_golf_championship "2024 NCAA Division I men's golf championship").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-MG-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-18) Two Tigers have won individual NCAA Championships: Charles Warren in 1997 and Turk Pettit in 2021.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-MG-17)2009 U.S. Open champion Lucas Glover also played golf at Clemson.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-19)

### Discontinued varsity sports
Swimming & Diving  
The Tigers men's swimming & diving team was established in 1919, and won the Southern Conference championship in 1939, and the ACC team championship in 1986. The women's swimming & diving team began in 1975, and won 4 ACC championships (1987, 1988, 1989, 1997), and Mitzi Kremer won 4 NCAA championships. Both swimming teams and men's diving were discontinued after the 2012 season, and women's diving was discontinued after 2017.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlackman_et_al.2013209%E2%80%93217-35)
Wrestling  
Wrestling at Clemson University was discontinued in 1995, despite the success of the program, due to financial shortages from Tiger Athletics' funding from the university. The wrestling program began in 1975 winning the ACC title as a team under coach Eddie Griffin in 1991. The Tiger wrestling program produced eight All-Americans, two NCAA Champions, and a finish at the NCAA Championships as high as 7th in 1994.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-36)Noel Loban won Clemson's first national title in 1980, and went on to win a bronze medal in the 1984 Olympics. Sammie Henson is a former standout at Clemson, as one of the most accomplished Tiger wrestlers, with 1993 and 1994 NCAA Champion titles, who eventually earned a 2000 Olympics silver medal and became a World Champion in 1998 in freestyle wrestling.

The **Clemson Tigers football** program are the American football team at Clemson University. The Tigers compete in the NCAA Division IFootball Bowl Subdivision (FBS) of the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) of the Atlantic Coast Conference (ACC).

Formed in 1896, the program has an all-time record of 804–473–44,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-2) with a bowl record of 27–23. Clemson was a College Football Playoff finalist in 2015, 2016, 2018, and 2019, defeating Alabama in both 2016 and 2018 to secure the national title. Clemson has had six undefeated seasons (including the first-ever 15–0 team), boasted six consecutive playoff appearances from 2015 to 2021, and retains 27 conference championships, including 8 since 2011. Its alumni include over 100 All-Americans, 17 Academic All-Americans and over 250 players in the National Football League.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-4) Clemson has had eight members inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame: players Banks McFadden, Terry Kinard, Jeff Davis, and C. J. Spiller along with coaches John Heisman, Jess Neely, Frank Howard, and Danny Ford.

Clemson is one of the founding members of the ACC and holds 22 ACC titles, the most of any member. Its 28 total conference titles, including six consecutive ACC titles from 2015 to 2020, are the most of any ACC school. Clemson's most recent ACC title came in 2024, against SMU. Clemson's streak of eleven consecutive 10-win seasons from 2011-2022 ranked second in active streaks behind the Alabama Crimson Tide, coming to an end after Clemson's 2023 season where they finished with a 9–4 record.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-6) Among its eight undefeated regular seasons, Clemson has been crowned national champion 3 times. Clemson was named poll-era national champion and finished with its third perfect season with a win over Nebraska in the 1982 Orange Bowl. Clemson was the National Championship Finalist Runner-up with a 14–1 record in 2015 before winning the National Title over No. 1 Alabama in college football's first National Championship rematch in 2016, and again in 2018. However, Clemson then lost the next year to the undefeated LSU Tigers in the 2020 College Football Playoff National Championship 25-42. The Tigers have 46 bowl appearances, 20 of which are among the [New Year's Six](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Year's_Six "New Year's Six") Bowls, including nine during the "Big Four" era. Clemson has 34 finishes in the final top 25 in the modern era and it finished in either the Associated Press final poll or the coaches' final poll a combined 59 times since 1939.
The Tigers play their home games in Memorial Stadium on the university's Clemson, South Carolina campus. The stadium's nickname, "Death Valley" was coined in 1948 by Presbyterian College head coach Lonnie McMillan after his teams were routinely defeated there. Memorial Stadium is among the largest stadiums in college football.
Walter Riggs, the "father of Clemson football"

Walter Riggs, often regarded as the "father of Clemson football," brought the sport to Clemson from the Agricultural and Mechanical College of Alabama (now Auburn University). The team's first game, played on Halloween 1896, resulted in a 2–1 record for the inaugural season. Riggs influenced the choice of the team mascot and colors. The Tigers’ early success included their first undefeated season in 1900 under coach John W. Heisman, who led the team to a 19–3–2 record. Heisman’s coaching set a precedent for excellence and innovation.
During the mid-20th century, the program experienced substantial growth under Frank Howard, who coached from 1940 to 1969. Howard's tenure saw Clemson win two Southern Conference championships and six ACC championships. Known for his colorful personality and imaginative storytelling, Howard integrated various offensive formations. His legacy includes the tradition of rubbing "Howard's Rock" before home games and the naming of the playing field at Memorial Stadium as "Frank Howard Field" in 1974.
The late 20th century and early 21st century saw the football program navigate through challenges and successes under multiple head coaches. Danny Ford led the Tigers to their first national championship in 1981, achieving an undefeated season. Ford's era was marked by NCAA sanctions due to recruiting violations, which impacted the program's reputation and success. Ken Hatfield, Ford’s successor, focused on cleaning up the program's image but faced criticism from fans, leading to his resignation. Subsequent coaches, including Tommy West, struggled to achieve consistent success until the hiring of Tommy Bowden in 1999, who maintained bowl eligibility every season, but failed to secure an ACC championship.
Coach Dabo Swinney

The modern era is defined by the leadership of Dabo Swinney, who became head coach in 2008. Swinney revitalized the program, leading the Tigers to multiple ACC championships and two national titles in 2016 and 2018. His tenure has been characterized by significant achievements, including the establishment of Clemson as a perennial contender in the College Football Playoff. Swinney’s ability to recruit and develop talent, combined with strategic hires like offensive coordinator Chad Morris and defensive coordinator Brent Venables, has sustained Clemson’s success. Notably, under Swinney, Clemson became the first team since 1897 to finish a season 15–0. In 2022, Clemson defeated Syracuse 27–21, extending the Tigers' home winning streak to 38, a new ACC record.

Clemson won the Southern Intercollegiate Athletic Association in 1900 and 1902 (tied 1903 and 1906) along with the Southern Conference title in 1940 and 1948.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-10) Their 22 ACC titles (20 outright, 2 tied) are the most ACC football championships._[citation needed_]_[when?_] In 1965, South Carolina violated participation rules relating to two ineligible players and was required to forfeit wins against North Carolina State and Clemson.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-mediaguidelist-11) North Carolina State and Clemson were then declared co-champions.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers_football#cite_note-12)

As of 2018, the Tiger baseball team has posted a combined 32 ACC regular season and tournament championships (the most in the conference), 43 NCAA Tournament appearances, 17 NCAA Regional Titles, four NCAA Super Regional titles, and 12 College World Series appearances. Much of the baseball program's success occurred under Bill Wilhelm during his 35 seasons as Clemson's head coach. Erik Bakich is the Tigers' current head coach, having replaced Monte Lee after the conclusion of the 2022 season.

The Clemson men's basketball team has qualified for the [NCAA Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_men's_basketball_tournament "NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament") 13 times, and reached the Sweet 16 four times and the Elite Eight once. They are currently coached by Brad Brownell since 2010.
The Clemson women's basketball team began in 1975, and saw its biggest success in the late 1980s and 1990s. The Tigers reached the NCAA Elite Eight in 1991, and the Sweet Sixteen three times (1989, 1990, 1999). Women's basketball won two [ACC Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACC_women's_basketball_tournament "ACC women's basketball tournament") championships in 1996 and 1999, and the regular season title in 1981. The team is currently coached by Amanda Butler.
The Tigers take the field by running down the hill in Memorial Stadium's east end zone, 2006.
Clemson has three national championships in football, the most recent coming in 2018 with a victory over Alabama 44–16 in the 2019 College Football Playoff National Championship. Clemson has appeared in the last six playoffs and won two national championships during those visits. The Tigers also possess the most Atlantic Coast Conference championships with 20, including winning the last six.
It has also won greater than 60% of its games, placing it in the top 25 on the all-time winning percentage list. Clemson also won two Southern Conference titles before joining the ACC. The 1981 squad, led by Head Coach Danny Ford, became the first athletic team in school history to win a national championship. Clemson defeated Nebraska 22–15 in the Orange Bowl in Miami, Florida, to win the 1981 NCAA Football National Championship. Stars of the game included Homer Jordan (QB) and Perry Tuttle (WR). Clemson finished the year 12–0 and ranked #1 in the Associated Press and Coaches polls.

Some of the most notable coaching names in Clemson football history are John Heisman (who also coached at Akron, Auburn, Georgia Tech, Penn, Washington & Jefferson, and Rice; the Heisman Trophy is named after him), Jess Neely, Frank Howard (whom the playing field at Death Valley is named after), and Danny Ford. After Tommy Bowden resigned midseason on October 13, 2008, Dabo Swinney took over as interim head coach.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-ESPN-13) On December 1, 2008, Swinney was named head coach of the Clemson Tigers football team.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-14)
Before each home game, the team ends pre-game warm ups and proceeds to the locker room. With five minutes to go before game time, three buses leave the street behind the West Endzone carrying the Clemson football players. The buses pull to a stop at the gate in front of The Hill, and the Tigers gather at the top, where each player proceeds to rub "Howard's Rock", which is an imported rock from Death Valley, California that was presented to Frank Howard in 1967. While Tiger Rag is played and a cannon sounds, the Tigers run down the hill onto the field in front of over 83,000 screaming fans. This tradition has been dubbed "The most exciting 25 seconds in college football" by sportscaster Brent Musburger.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-15)

The Tiger men's golf team have a tradition of being among the best in the ACC and the nation, having won several ACC titles and regularly qualifying for the NCAA Tournament. In 2003, Clemson defeated Oklahoma State to win its first [National Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_Men's_Golf_Championships "NCAA Division I Men's Golf Championships") in golf and the 4th overall for the school.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-Golf_2003_NC-16) In addition to that victory, Clemson also won the ACC and NCAA East Regional titles that year, making the Tigers the first program in NCAA history to win its conference, regional, and national championship tournaments in the same year.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-Golf_2003_NC-16) Clemson has also won eight regional titles since the NCAA adopted the regional tournament format in 1989, with their most recent win coming in [2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_NCAA_Division_I_men's_golf_championship "2024 NCAA Division I men's golf championship").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-MG-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-18) Two Tigers have won individual NCAA Championships: Charles Warren in 1997 and Turk Pettit in 2021.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-MG-17)2009 U.S. Open champion Lucas Glover also played golf at Clemson.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-19)

The Tigers men's swimming & diving team was established in 1919, and won the Southern Conference championship in 1939, and the ACC team championship in 1986. The women's swimming & diving team began in 1975, and won 4 ACC championships (1987, 1988, 1989, 1997), and Mitzi Kremer won 4 NCAA championships. Both swimming teams and men's diving were discontinued after the 2012 season, and women's diving was discontinued after 2017.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_Tigers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlackman_et_al.2013209%E2%80%93217-35)
Wrestling  
Wrestling at Clemson University was discontinued in 1995, despite the success of the program, due to financial shortages from Tiger Athletics' funding from the university. Sammie Henson is a former standout at Clemson, as one of the most accomplished Tiger wrestlers, with 1993 and 1994 NCAA Champion titles, who eventually earned a 2000 Olympics silver medal and became a World Champion in 1998 in freestyle wrestling.

Title: Democrats Just Won an Impressive Senate Majority. But It Could’ve Been Even Bigger.
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7
The Slatest

## Please allow us a bit of Wednesday-morning quarterbacking.
Nov 13, 2026 5:45 AM
Photo illustration by Slate. Photos by Joe Raedle/Getty Images, Scott Olson/Getty Images, William Campbell/Getty Images, andjamieforlouisiana.com.
_This story is adapted from the Slatest newsletter. You can__sign up here__to get it in your inbox every day._
For Democrats, the past two weeks have been one long celebration. The party officially clinched its 55 th Senate seat on Wednesday night and remains on track to win a 56 th as election officials continue to count ballots in Alaska. Senators and strategists are already salivating over the prospect of winning 60 seats or more come 2028, a majority that would be big enough to override Republican filibusters.
But could they actually have gotten one sooner? But for a little more party coordination, slightly better candidates, and a smidge more money, there’s a strong case that Democrats could be basking in a 60-seat majority right now. Let’s take a look at four Senate races where the party came tantalizingly close last week—and at how things could have turned out differently.
Video from Slate

## Please allow us a bit of Wednesday-morning quarterbacking.
#### **A Failure to Coordinate in Montana**
At first glance, Big Sky Country doesn’t look like much of a missed opportunity for Democrats. After all, Republican Kurt Alme ran more than 10 points ahead of Seth Bodnar, his closest challenger. But Bodnar was running as an independent, and the Democrat who won the primary, Alani Bankhead, rebuffed repeated calls to drop out to avoid splitting the vote. Alme ended up winning with just 48 percent of ballots cast, so it’s quite possible that Bodnar would have beaten him had Bankhead shelved her ego.
She isn’t the only person at fault, though. Bodnar, a former Democrat, could have chosen to run under the party standard. If he had instead beaten Bankhead in the Democratic primary, it’s possible he’d have gone on to defeat Alme with a D next to his name. There are no sure things with any of these races, but the divided vote certainly didn’t help.

## Please allow us a bit of Wednesday-morning quarterbacking.
#### **A Recruiting Flop in Louisiana**
Democrats put up an impressive showing across the South, padding their majority by winning seats in Texas, North and South Carolina, Georgia, and Mississippi. They nearly pulled off the same thing in nearby Louisiana, where Jamie Davis, a Democratic third-generation farmer, lost to Republican Rep. Julia Letlow by less than 2 points. Neither party expected Louisiana to be competitive, and the fact that Davis made it a race despite getting zilch from Senate Democratic leadership suggests that even a relatively small cash infusion could’ve put him over the top.
But it’s also possible that the seeds of Democrats’ defeat were planted last year after Chuck Schumer, the Senate Democratic leader, tried and failed to convince John Bel Edwards, a former Louisiana governor, to run. Edwards, a conservative Democrat who supports gun rights and opposes abortion, has repeatedly defied the odds in this deep-red state, winning reelection in 2019 despite Donald Trump’s efforts to boost his opponent. Had Edwards heeded Schumer, he might now be headed to Washington.

## Please allow us a bit of Wednesday-morning quarterbacking.
#### **A Money Shortfall in Florida**
No other state has disappointed Democrats so consistently in the Trump era—which made it all the more surprising when a Democrat nearly flipped one of its Senate seats last week. Angie Nixon, a state lawmaker who won the Democratic primary in an upset and then ran an energetic general-election campaign, ended up falling to Sen. Ashley Moody by less than 3 points. Nixon’s performance is even more impressive when you consider that she’s a democratic socialist who ran on an unapologetically progressive platform and that national Democratic leaders spent little to help her.
That fact has invited charges that Schumer and his colleagues were scared away by Nixon’s progressivism—or even by the fact that she’s Black. But there are a few caveats worth considering. For one thing, the Democratic nominee for governor this year was so white and moderate that he was actually a former Republican—yet he still lost, despite coming closer than Nixon did. Florida is also an incredibly expensive patchwork of media markets, and diverting resources to fund ads on Nixon’s behalf could well have come at the expense of other, more winnable races.

## Please allow us a bit of Wednesday-morning quarterbacking.
#### **A Strategic Fail in Nebraska**
The Cornhusker State is another place where Democrats cleared the decks for an independent candidate who ended up falling flat. Dan Osborn, a former union leader and Navy veteran, first ran for Senate in 2024, losing to the GOP incumbent by nearly 7 points. Last week, despite running in a far bluer political environment, Osborn did just half a point better.
It’s certainly possible that only a candidate with an R next to their name can win a state Trump swept by 20 points. But the states that appear to have most stubbornly resisted last week’s blue wave—Montana, Nebraska, and South Dakota—also happen to be places where many Democrats threw their weight behind independent candidates who they believed had a better shot of winning in deep-red territory. It might be time for the party to rethink that particular strategy.

## Please allow us a bit of Wednesday-morning quarterbacking.
#### **The Lesson**
What to make of these near misses? Some Democrats might be tempted to read them as an indictment of Schumer and other Senate leaders’ decisions—especially if they’re angling to replace them. Yet that might be a bit harsh. Even the most optimistic political observers didn’t foresee the magnitude of the electorate’s shift, and investing heavily in long-shot states early would have invited criticisms that Democrats were abandoning more traditional battlegrounds. The truth is that election cycles are often littered with missed opportunities. Shoulda woulda couldas aside, money, attention, and quality candidates are finite—and even seemingly small decisions can end up having a big political impact.
Tolga Akdoğan
**I know it’s been a politics-heavy couple of weeks, so let’s pivot to my colleagues’ suggestions about what to read to take your mind off the midterms:**
**A wonder drug that wasn’t:** In 1977 a “miracle cure” for cancer began to take hold in America. Though it had been dismissed by doctors as ineffective and potentially dangerous, laetrile was everywhere, and so was the controversy over it. The story of one little boy who was diagnosed with cancer shows the far-reaching consequences of a craze that has clear echoes today. Evan Chung recounts the family’s story and talks to the mother at the center of it all about how her decisions haunt her now.
**Some juicy details from the Watergate era:** Bob Woodward’s new tell-all book, _Secrets: A Reporter’s Memoir_, is full of revelations both professional and personal. Most tantalizingly, Woodward names many of the sources whose stories helped bring down Richard Nixon’s presidency. Fred Kaplan calls it “catnip for newshounds and gossipmongers!”
**A mental health reminder:** It’s become a common refrain that men would rather do almost anything than go to therapy. Unfortunately, there’s a kernel of truth to this meme. Ted Scheinman shares why men so often keep their struggles bottled up—and how cathartic it can be to tell your friends that you’re struggling with depression.

## Please allow us a bit of Wednesday-morning quarterbacking.
#### **The Lesson**
**The music video that changed MTV:** For years, Black musicians had a fraught relationship with MTV, with its lily-white lineup of artists and allegiance to white listeners. Michael Jackson made inroads with “Billie Jean,” but it took Whitney Houston for there to be a real breakthrough on the channel. Brandon Tensley breaks down how Houston’s music videos ushered in a new era for pop music.
**OK, that’s it from me. Enjoy your day!**

## 11:42 a.m. EST
### Millions of voters face new laws at ballot box
More than three dozen voting laws passed in Republican-controlled states are taking effect for the first time this year, many of them containing elements of proposals that Trump tried unsuccessfully to get through Congress.
At the state level, the changes include new requirements to show proof of citizenship. College students in New Hampshire won't be using college IDs. Iowa voters without ID can't count on other voters to vouch for them, and some voters in Mississippi might need birth certificates or passports for verification. Naturalized citizens might get to polling places and learn they've been purged because databases used to check their citizenship against voter registration lists are outdated.
**READ MORE:** 5 expert takeaways on 2026 midterm election security
Opponents say the restrictions make it harder for eligible voters to vote. Republican lawmakers who support the tighter voting laws, especially around voter ID, say they help build trust in elections.

## 11:42 a.m. EST
### The Texas governor's race has focused on a new lightning rod: data centers
A campaign sign for Democratic Texas gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa near a polling station during the midterm elections, on Election Day, in Austin, Texas, Nov. 3, 2026. Photo by Mike Segar/ Reuters
Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who has comfortably held the governor's mansion since 2014, is in one of his tougher fights. He faces Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa in an election year favoring her party.
The race, still an uphill slog for Hinojosa, has revolved around the standard concerns of high costs and public education, but the hulking structures that power artificial intelligence butted in. Data centers have drawn bipartisan anger from Americans who live by them and concerns that the buildings guzzle too much water and electricity.
Last year, Abbott celebrated Google's investments partly to build data centers in the state. Hinojosa hammered him for it, arguing that it represented the influence of wealthy people over everyday Texans. The governor has since shifted his position, ordering the pause of data center permits and saying, "Texans come first."

## 11:11 a.m. EST
### Flooding prompts relocation of some polling places in Florida
Some voters in Florida were being directed to cast their ballots in new places on Tuesday after their polling sites were relocated due to continued rain and flooding.
Florida elections officials said 21 polling places in eight counties were moved. The relocations were mostly along the central and southern Atlantic coast, with some inland counties included. County officials said they notified voters by text and email, and signs were posted at voting locations directing people to the new sites.
Some residents expressed frustration and concern on social media that some voters may not be able to get to the polls because of flooding.
Amy Keith, the Florida state director for Common Cause, said the flooding is a big issue.
"Today it has already been a pretty challenging morning," she said, urging voters to double-check their voting locations with election supervisors.

## 11:11 a.m. EST
### Schumer says he's 'nauseously optimistic'
After casting his vote at a Brooklyn school, Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer said he was optimistic that when polls close, "there will be a new Democratic majority in the United States Senate."
"We don't want to count our chickens before they hatch. So I'd characterize our mood as nauseously optimistic," Schumer said.
He predicted that Democrat Abdul El-Sayed would win the U.S. Senate race in Michigan, despite the decision by his former primary opponent, U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, to endorse Republican Mike Rogers.
**WATCH LIVE:** House Democratic Leader Jeffries holds Election Day news conference
"She's one vote," Schumer said. "He's going to win tonight because he's talking about what Michiganders care about."
Schumer said that a year ago, no one thought the Democrats might be in a position to retake the Senate. But he credited the party's "relentless" focus on affordability and "chaos overseas in a war with Iran that nobody wants" with making Democrats more competitive.

## 11:11 a.m. EST
### A look at recent midterm election results
Midterm elections generally favor the party that doesn't hold the White House, but the two most recent cycles generated a mixed result.
When Joe Biden was president, Republicans won control of the House in 2022, picking up nine seats and assuming a slim majority. But Democrats maintained control of the Senate and even picked up a seat in the chamber.
A similar dynamic occurred during Trump's first term, though the gains were much larger for Democrats in the House. They netted 40 seats in the 2018 midterms and took the majority for the first time in eight years. Still, Republicans expanded their Senate majority by two seats.
Some analysts see similarities between this midterm political environment and that of 2006, when President George W. Bush and Republicans faced headwinds from high fuel prices and the war in Iraq. That year, Democrats added 30 House seats and six Senate seats to take the majority in both chambers.

## 10:36 a.m. EST
### Massive spending and presidential visits signal Ohio is back in play
After years of having its storied bellwether status written off, Ohio is competitive again.
Republicans should have run away with critical contests for U.S. Senate and governor, based on Trump's three consecutive sweeping victories in the state. Instead, they headed into Election Day in close contests with their Democratic rivals.
**WATCH:** Campaigns spend big to sway voters with increasingly personal attack ads
Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown has mounted a comeback bid against Republican U.S. Sen. Jon Husted, appointed last year to the seat formerly held by Vice President JD Vance. Both Trump and Vance visited Ohio in the campaign's closing weeks to rally voters, as did former President Barack Obama for Democrats.
The governor's contest pits Republican biotech entrepreneur Vivek Ramaswamy against Democrat Dr. Amy Acton, the state's former COVID-era health director.
An ad Ramaswamy ran featuring Acton's estranged mother became a flashpoint in the race and across the U.S.

## 10:36 a.m. EST
### Ukraine's Zelenskyy warns of massive Russian strikes as the world focuses on U.S. midterms
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that Russia will step up massive drone and missile strikes on his country's energy facilities this week while international attention is focused on the U.S. midterm elections.
"The world will be watching the American midterms, and what is happening here in Ukraine, along with our difficulties with air defense and Patriot missiles, will be overlooked," he said in an evening video post.
Video 52
Russian ballistic missiles and drones damaged energy facilities in 10 Ukrainian regions Tuesday — part of a campaign by Moscow to pressure Kyiv over the winter months.

## 10:36 a.m. EST
### General mood of the country from AP-NORC polling
Americans have been in a sour mood about the country's direction for several years, according to AP-NORC polling.
About 7 in 10 U.S. adults say the country is heading in the wrong direction, according to AP-NORC polling from September. Only about one-quarter of U.S. adults say things are headed in the "right direction." Democrats and independents are much likelier than Republicans to say things are not going the right way.
**READ MORE:** Election Day underway after a surge in early voting, as Trump sows doubt on results
Roughly 6 in 10 U.S. adults say they are feeling "very" or "somewhat" pessimistic about the state of politics in this country, according to an AP-NORC poll from October. About half are feeling negatively about the future of democracy in the U.S.

## 10:36 a.m. EST
### U.S. will halt $4B in aid to Israel as ally shifts to buying military hardware, Trump says
The Republican president told Fox News Channel during an Election Day telephone interview that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had approached him about the idea and that they have been talking about it for a couple of years.
Trump said Israel doesn't need the aid and that it's a lot of money for the U.S. to spend. But Trump also said the aid had become a Democratic talking point for candidates such as Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.
**READ MORE:** Trump says U.S. will stop giving $4 billion in aid to Israel next year
"We give them $4 billion of things and money, and they don't need it," Trump said.
Netanyahu's office had no immediate comment.
The United States has sent tens of billions of dollars in military aid to Israel over the past few years.

## 10:36 a.m. EST
### Sen. Susan Collins tries to keep her seat while fending off Troy Jackson
Collins is running for her sixth term on a pledge to continue serving Maine as one of the few remaining moderates in the Senate.
The Republican faces a challenge from Democrat Troy Jackson, who entered the race late. Jackson has tried to paint Collins as too close to Trump, while Collins has touted her willingness to break from the rest of the Republican Party on key votes.
Video 53
Collins is the only Republican senator from New England, and she has triumphed in previous tough elections.
This time, Democrats focused on unseating her from the beginning, but the party's June primary winner, Graham Platner, withdrew from the race after facing sexual assault allegations that he denied.
Jackson became the new nominee after winning a special nominating convention in late July.

## 10:36 a.m. EST
### Justice Department dispatches 1,000 election monitors to the polls
The Justice Department announced early Tuesday that it is sending roughly 1,000 federal election monitors to all 50 states to observe Election Day voting.
Many are expected in populated areas that tend to vote for Democrats. They include past hot spots for election tensions, like Detroit, Philadelphia and Georgia's Fulton County.
The monitoring program isn't new, but it has faced criticism from voting rights groups concerned about federal interference and voter intimidation.
The NAACP sued after the department said it would include law enforcement officers in the program, but a judge ruled against the group overnight, arguing the government had made it clear that monitors would be in plainclothes, would not carry firearms and wouldn't have the power to make arrests at poll sites.
The Justice Department has said its monitors will observe and will not interfere with voting.

## 10:36 a.m. EST
### House races playing out deep in Trump country
People leave a polling station at a town hall during the midterm elections, in Bramwell, West Virginia, on Nov. 3, 2026. Photo by Marcus Constantino/ Reuters
A campaign sign for Democratic Texas gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa near a polling station during the US midterm elections, on Election Day, in Austin, Texas, US, November 3, 2026. REUTERS/Mike Segar
Republicans are mostly on defense in the battle for control of the U.S. House.
Most of the top battlegrounds are districts Trump won in 2024, sometimes by a lot.
Republicans and allied groups pulled spending from several House races in October, shifting, for example, away from GOP incumbents in Iowa and New Jersey.
At Trump's urging, Republicans in states including Texas and Florida tried to give themselves a boost with early redistricting, but that may turn out to be a flop.
Democrats are defending a handful of seats in Trump country as well, and there are pockets of potential GOP upside around the country.
The AP has a detailed rundown of the House districts in play and the fight for the majority.

## 10:36 a.m. EST
### Senate control up for grabs in states Trump carried
Control of the Senate hangs in the balance in a way few could have foreseen.
Originally, Democrats believed they only had a narrow path to the majority, and their plan required flipping seats in Alaska, Ohio, Maine and North Carolina.
However, the map has shifted, and Democrats believe they have a shot at Texas, Kansas and Iowa as well.
**READ MORE:** 13 races that will determine control of the Senate
Many of these are states Trump won by double-digit margins two years ago.
Democrats need to play defense as well. Although they're expected to hold Georgia, they also need to lock down Michigan and Minnesota.

## 10:36 a.m. EST
### In Maine, a voter feels 'the weight of the world'
In Falmouth, Maine, 60-year-old Susan Myers said she's optimistic that Senate candidate Troy Jackson can take advantage of anti-Trump sentiment and defeat longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins. She's also aware of how recent elections have gone for diehard Democrats like herself.
"I'm hopeful. I feel like there's been so much disappointment these last few election cycles that I don't want to get my hopes up," she said.
**LIVE RESULTS:** Maine Senate midterm election
Myers voted early at Falmouth Town Hall and was picking up an absentee ballot for her daughter.
She said so much national attention on Maine this election has been overwhelming. The Senate race is one of this year's most competitive and could decide which party controls the chamber.
"It feels a little bit like we have the weight of the world on our shoulders," Myers said.

## 10:36 a.m. EST
### Latinos form a crucial bloc of swing voters
Latinos helped return Trump to the White House in 2024. Now they're poised to play an outsized role in the midterms.
The path to a U.S. House majority runs through heavily Latino districts in states such as Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida and Texas. The front-line Senate race in Texas likewise could hinge on Latinos.
**WATCH:** GOP's big bet on Texas Latino voters could backfire in midterms
About 6 in 10 Hispanic adults disapprove of Trump's handling of the presidency, according to an Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll from October. About 7 in 10 disapprove of his performance on the economy.
One key factor will be how effective Democrats have been at making the case for themselves. Will disaffected Trump supporters vote for Democrats, or just sit out the midterms?

## 10:36 a.m. EST
### In Michigan's Senate race, history and control of the chamber are on the line
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is seeking to become the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. Republican Mike Rogers wants to be the first member of his party to win a Michigan Senate race in more than three decades.
The contest to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters is among a handful that could determine which party controls the Senate.
Video 54
Although Michigan Democrats have been successful in recent midterm elections, Trump carried the battleground state in two of his three campaigns. That divided political landscape helped set the stage for one of the most bitter and contentious Senate races of the cycle.
El-Sayed has accused Rogers of being a "puppet" for Trump. Rogers has accused El-Sayed of having ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, while Trump has falsely called the Democrat a "jihadist."
Progressives are hoping an El-Sayed victory will signal their agenda can resonate in a battleground state ahead of the next presidential election.

## 10:36 a.m. EST
### Millions of Americans will be voting in new congressional districts
Mid-decade redistricting shook up the House map ahead of the midterms, changing the boundaries of around one-third of congressional districts.
The AP analyzed each district's 2024 presidential vote margin before and after redistricting and found that while many individual districts saw dramatic shifts in partisanship and demographic makeup, the national U.S. House map did not shift significantly toward either party.
Learn more about how redistricting shaped the 2026 midterm elections and see how your district boundaries changed in this map.

## 10:36 a.m. EST
### Midterm results will chart the course of Trump's final two years
Trump is staring down twin threats from Capitol Hill for his last two years as president if his party loses at least one chamber in Tuesday's midterms: investigations and impeachment.
Democratic lawmakers are eager to exercise oversight, with senior officials long telegraphing how they would go after an administration they believe has escaped accountability for policies, personal profits and abuses of power.
The majority party controls gavels on powerful House committees, which come with larger staff budgets and more expansive resources, including subpoena powers.
Less certain are prospects for impeaching Trump, although House Democratic leaders will almost certainly come under pressure from their left flank to do so. Rather than Trump, who was impeached twice during his first term but acquitted by the Senate both times, Democrats may instead try to impeach Cabinet officials.
If Republicans lose the Senate, Trump's ability to push his judicial and executive branch nominees through to confirmation will also be severely weakened.
